\begin{center}
{\LARGE\bfseries Foundations: quantum-information preliminaries, number model, exact admissibility and emission}\\[4pt]
{\large Contract, version 0.12.0}
\end{center}
\begin{overview}
The foundations module states the arithmetic every other module relies on, and none of its mathematics is specific to a protocol; one emission rule names the data of a protocol declaration it binds. A \termref{term-declared-value}{declared value} is a binary64 number and denotes exactly the dyadic rational it is; a sum is accumulated in a \termref{term-declared-order}{declared order} and \termref{term-rounds-nowhere}{rounds nowhere} when each of its binary64 additions is exact, which makes it the exact sum (\hyperlink{claim-foundations/lem:exact-accumulation}{Lemma~\ref*{lem:exact-accumulation}}). A declared operator family is \termref{term-exactly-admissible}{exactly admissible} for a \termref{term-sector-map}{sector map} when it is exactly Hermitian, positive and complete, with a completeness sum that rounds nowhere (\hyperlink{claim-foundations/def:exact-admissibility}{Definition~\ref*{def:exact-admissibility}}). The requirements say who establishes this: declared operator data are exactly admissible at every \termref{term-module-boundary}{module boundary} (\hyperlink{claim-foundations/req:boundary-admission}{Requirement~\ref*{req:boundary-admission}}), every consumer decides its predicates exactly and refuses otherwise, and a producer verifies what it emits before emitting it (\hyperlink{claim-foundations/req:exact-emission}{Requirement~\ref*{req:exact-emission}}). One \termref{term-declared-tolerance}{declared tolerance} per instance bounds only how far an instance may move its own declaration, only a declarer snaps its data onto its lattice, and a snap of a measurement family keeps the blocks known exactly on the lattice and moves the others by one fidelity-first procedure that revives no zero (\hyperlink{claim-foundations/req:snap-reference}{Requirement~\ref*{req:snap-reference}}). A moved block is related to its model by no claim, so a run evaluates it off its snap, with the reference handed beside the snap in its place (\hyperlink{claim-foundations/def:evaluated-off-snap}{Definition~\ref*{def:evaluated-off-snap}}), or rests there on a named assumption (\hyperlink{claim-foundations/ass:snapped-measurement}{Assumption~\ref*{ass:snapped-measurement}}) unless it declares the strict option that refuses it; the module fixes the \termref{term-exact-island}{exact island}, the bounds that carry a least eigenvalue, a rank and a matrix function across an enclosure, and the three tiers of a reported key rate. Beside the arithmetic it states the \termref{term-round-model}{round model}, with its \termref{term-attack-set}{attack sets} and the round homogeneity the modules' round assumptions assert, and the quantum-information preliminaries the entropy optimisation is written in: pinching, the sandwiched R\'enyi divergence and its conditional entropies, the classical divergences and the quantum relative entropy, the extended divergence kernel (\hyperlink{claim-foundations/lem:kernel}{Lemma~\ref*{lem:kernel}}), the bound by which pinching lowers the trace power (\hyperlink{claim-foundations/lem:pinchmono}{Lemma~\ref*{lem:pinchmono}}), and two published results on pinched trace powers (\hyperlink{claim-foundations/fact:pinch-id}{Fact~\ref*{fact:pinch-id}}, \hyperlink{claim-foundations/fact:concavity}{Fact~\ref*{fact:concavity}}). The module's main claims are \hyperlink{claim-foundations/lem:exact-accumulation}{Lemma~\ref*{lem:exact-accumulation}}, \hyperlink{claim-foundations/def:exact-admissibility}{Definition~\ref*{def:exact-admissibility}} and \hyperlink{claim-foundations/req:boundary-admission}{Requirement~\ref*{req:boundary-admission}} on the side of the arithmetic, and \hyperlink{claim-foundations/lem:kernel}{Lemma~\ref*{lem:kernel}} and \hyperlink{claim-foundations/lem:pinchmono}{Lemma~\ref*{lem:pinchmono}} on the side of the entropy optimisation. It reads nothing from another module, and the strengthenings of exact admissibility that a module states for its own data, such as a declared lattice or conditions on Alice's data, stay with that module.
\end{overview}

\section*{Main results}\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Main results}
\sectionintro{The module's most important results, those its overview names as what it establishes, with every assumption each rests on, directly or through the claims it uses. Each links to its statement and proof; the statements digest holds them in full.}
\par\noindent\hyperref[lem:kernel]{\textbf{Lemma~\ref*{lem:kernel}}}\enspace Extended divergence kernel\par\nobreak
{\small\itshape\color{nnGrey}\noindent The divergence kernel d(u, v) = u log\ensuremath{_{2}}(u/v), extended to vanishing arguments, is jointly convex, lower semicontinuous and non-increasing in v. These properties keep the objective well defined at support boundaries and let it be composed with concave branch quantities.\par}\nobreak
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Rests on}no assumption}
\par\noindent\hyperref[lem:pinchmono]{\textbf{Lemma~\ref*{lem:pinchmono}}}\enspace Pinching lowers the trace power\par\nobreak
{\small\itshape\color{nnGrey}\noindent For \ensuremath{\alpha} \textgreater{} 1, pinching the \ensuremath{\alpha}-th root of a positive semidefinite operator and raising the result to the power \ensuremath{\alpha} never increases the trace, and leaves it unchanged exactly when the operator is block diagonal for the pinching. This bounds the trace-power terms of the MEAT objective.\par}\nobreak
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Rests on}no assumption}
\par\noindent\hyperref[lem:exact-accumulation]{\textbf{Lemma~\ref*{lem:exact-accumulation}}}\enspace Exactness of a sum that rounds nowhere\par\nobreak
{\small\itshape\color{nnGrey}\noindent A sequential sum rounds nowhere exactly when every exact partial sum is a binary64 number, and then the computed sum equals the exact sum at every step. A predicate stated on such a sum is a predicate on the declared values themselves.\par}\nobreak
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Rests on}no assumption}
\par\noindent\hyperref[def:exact-admissibility]{\textbf{Definition~\ref*{def:exact-admissibility}}}\enspace Exact admissibility of a declared operator family\par\nobreak
{\small\itshape\color{nnGrey}\noindent A declared operator family is exactly admissible for a sector map with constant c when (T) its own sector map agrees, (H) every block is exactly Hermitian, (P) positive, (C) it sums to c times the identity and (S) its declared-order sum rounds nowhere. Each is a property of the declared numbers.\par}\nobreak
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Rests on}no assumption}
\par\noindent\hyperref[req:boundary-admission]{\textbf{Requirement~\ref*{req:boundary-admission}}}\enspace Exact admissibility at every module boundary\par\nobreak
{\small\itshape\color{nnGrey}\noindent Declared operator data cross every module boundary exactly admissible, so every sum a predicate reads is the exact sum. The declarer makes them so, or, for data an instance passes on unchanged, the consumer's exact decision on entry does, and a consumer that finds otherwise refuses them.\par}\nobreak
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Rests on}no assumption}

\section{Quantum-information preliminaries}\label{group-foundations/def:pinching}
\sectionintro{These are the quantum-information objects the entropy optimisation is written in: pinching, the sandwiched R\'enyi divergence with its two conditional entropies, and the classical divergences with the quantum relative entropy. The section's main results, two lemmas, establish what the optimisation needs of them, that the extended divergence kernel is jointly convex, lower semicontinuous and non-increasing in its second argument (\hyperlink{claim-foundations/lem:kernel}{Lemma~\ref*{lem:kernel}}), and that pinching lowers the trace power (\hyperlink{claim-foundations/lem:pinchmono}{Lemma~\ref*{lem:pinchmono}}). Two published results close the section, the pinched trace-power form of the conditional R\'enyi entropy (\hyperlink{claim-foundations/fact:pinch-id}{Fact~\ref*{fact:pinch-id}}) and the concavity of the pinched trace-power functional (\hyperlink{claim-foundations/fact:concavity}{Fact~\ref*{fact:concavity}}).}

% claim foundations/def:pinching
\claimsummary{foundations/def:pinching}{Operator, state and channel conventions, and the pinching of a complete family of orthogonal projectors, which deletes the coherences between their ranges. A pinching is a self-adjoint, idempotent, unital mixture of unitary conjugations whose fixed points are the block-diagonal operators.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/def:pinching}{Definition}{def:pinching}{Operator conventions and pinching}
\begin{definition}[Operator conventions and pinching]\label{def:pinching}
All Hilbert spaces are finite-dimensional. For a system label $A$,
$\Lin{A}$ is the space of linear operators on $\Hs{A}$, $\Pos{A}$ its
positive semidefinite operators, and $\Seq{A}$ and $\Sleq{A}$ the
normalized and the subnormalized states, of trace equal to one and at most
one. A channel is a CPTP map; an instrument branch is a CP
trace-non-increasing (CPTNI) map. For $X\in\Pos{A}$ and $p>0$, the power
$X^{p}$ is defined by functional calculus on the support of $X$ and by $0^p=0$
on its kernel; in particular $X^{p}$ is block-diagonal for any orthogonal
decomposition for which $X$ is.

For a family of orthogonal projectors $\{\Pi_j\}_{j}$ on $\Hs{Q}$ with
$\sum_j\Pi_j=\idon{Q}$, the associated \emph{pinching} is the channel
$\tau\mapsto\sum_j\Pi_j\tau\Pi_j$. A pinching is CPTP, self-adjoint as a
superoperator ($\tr[Y\,\mathcal{E}(W)]=\tr[\mathcal{E}(Y)\,W]$), idempotent,
and unital. An operator $X$ is a fixed point iff it is block-diagonal,
$X=\sum_j\Pi_jX\Pi_j$; functional calculus of a block-diagonal PSD operator
acts blockwise, so a pinching commutes with taking powers of its fixed
points. Each of these properties is a one-line computation from the form
$\sum_j\Pi_j(\cdot)\Pi_j$ and orthogonality of the $\Pi_j$;
self-adjointness is
$\tr[Y\sum_j\Pi_jW\Pi_j]=\tr[\sum_j\Pi_jY\Pi_j\,W]$ by cyclicity.

A pinching is a uniform mixture of unitary conjugations. Enumerate the
projectors as $\Pi_1,\dots,\Pi_m$, put $\zeta\coloneqq e^{2\pi i/m}$ and
$U_k\coloneqq\sum_{j=1}^{m}\zeta^{jk}\Pi_j$ for $k\in\{0,\dots,m-1\}$; each
$U_k$ is unitary, $U_kU_k^{\dagger}=\sum_j|\zeta^{jk}|^2\Pi_j=\idon{Q}$ by
orthogonality, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pinch-unitary-mixture}
  \sum_{j}\Pi_j X\Pi_j=\frac1m\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}U_kXU_k^{\dagger}
  \qquad\text{for every }X\in\Lin{Q},
\end{equation}
since the right-hand side is
$\sum_{j,j'}\big(\frac1m\sum_k\zeta^{(j-j')k}\big)\Pi_jX\Pi_{j'}$ and the
inner average is $1$ for $j=j'$ and $0$ otherwise. In particular a pinching
does not increase the operator norm, a mixture of unitary conjugates of $X$
having norm at most $\|X\|$.
\end{definition}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Used by}\mref{Lem.}{lem:pinchmono}, \mref{Fact}{fact:pinch-id}, \mref{Def.}{def:round-model}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/lem:b-derivative}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/lem:kraus-freedom}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/prop:a-neutral}

\metasep implemented

% claim foundations/def:renyi
\claimsummary{foundations/def:renyi}{The sandwiched R\'enyi divergence of order \ensuremath{\alpha} \textgreater{} 1 and the two conditional entropies it induces, one at the fixed marginal and one optimised over the marginal, in bits. The fixed-marginal entropy is no larger, so substituting it inside a lower bound is conservative, and the reverse substitution is not.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/def:renyi}{Definition}{def:renyi}{Sandwiched Rényi divergence and conditional entropies}
\claimleadin{%
The source \cite[Def.~5.2]{tomamichel2016finite} writes the two conditional
entropies of the following definition, its Eqs.~(5.18)--(5.19), with a
tilde, as \href{../../../spec/notation.md}{\nolinkurl{spec/notation.md}} does for the sandwiched family; the
pair it writes with an overline, its Eqs.~(5.16)--(5.17), is the Petz
family, which is a different quantity.
}
\begin{definition}[Sandwiched Rényi divergence and conditional entropies]
\label{def:renyi}
For $\alpha\in(1,\infty)$, $\rho\in\Sleq{AB}$ and $\sigma\in\Pos{AB}$, on the
same system,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sandwiched}
  \Dsand(\rho\,\|\,\sigma)\coloneqq\frac{1}{\alpha-1}\log_2
  \tr\!\left[\left(\sigma^{\frac{1-\alpha}{2\alpha}}\,\rho\,
  \sigma^{\frac{1-\alpha}{2\alpha}}\right)^{\alpha}\right]
\end{equation}
when $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\sigma$, and
$\Dsand(\rho\|\sigma)\coloneqq+\infty$ otherwise. The exponent
$\frac{1-\alpha}{2\alpha}$ is negative, and the power of $\sigma$ is taken on
its support and is zero on its kernel, as for the generalised inverse; where
$\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\sigma$, $\rho=P\rho P$
for the projector $P$ onto that support, so the value reads the power on the
support alone. For
$\rho_{AB}\in\Seq{AB}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Hdefs}
  \Hsanddown(A|B)_{\rho}\coloneqq-\Dsand(\rho_{AB}\,\|\,\idon{A}\otimes\rho_B),
  \qquad
  \Hsandup(A|B)_{\rho}\coloneqq-\inf_{\sigma_B\in\Seq{B}}
  \Dsand(\rho_{AB}\,\|\,\idon{A}\otimes\sigma_B).
\end{equation}
Both are in bits. These are the definitions of
\cite[Def.~5.2, Eqs.~(5.18)--(5.19)]{tomamichel2016finite}. Since the
infimum in \eqref{eq:Hdefs} includes $\sigma_B=\rho_B$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:arrow-order}
  \Hsanddown(A|B)_{\rho}\;\le\;\Hsandup(A|B)_{\rho}.
\end{equation}
The substitution $\Hsandup\to\Hsanddown$ inside a lower bound is therefore
conservative, and the reverse is not.
\end{definition}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Used by}\mref{Fact}{fact:pinch-id}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/fact:meat}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/lem:purifier-indep}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/prop:value-range}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/rem:alpha-domain}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/rem:losses}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/thm:accumulated-entropy}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/thm:keylength}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/thm:reduction}

% claim foundations/def:kl
\claimsummary{foundations/def:kl}{The base-2 Kullback\textendash{}Leibler and R\'enyi divergences of probability vectors and the quantum relative entropy, with their conventions at zero. The Kullback\textendash{}Leibler divergence, the statistics penalty of the MEAT objective, is non-negative and vanishes only at equal vectors.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/def:kl}{Definition}{def:kl}{Classical divergences and the quantum relative entropy}
\begin{definition}[Classical divergences and the quantum relative entropy]\label{def:kl}
For probability vectors $\mathbf q,\mathbf p$ on a finite alphabet,
$\sfD(\mathbf q\|\mathbf p)\coloneqq\sum_c q(c)\log_2\frac{q(c)}{p(c)}$ with
the conventions $0\log_2\frac{0}{p}=0$ and $q\log_2\frac{q}{0}=+\infty$ for
$q>0$. For $\alpha\in(1,\infty)$ the classical R\'enyi divergence is
$D_{\alpha}(\mathbf q\|\mathbf p)\coloneqq
\frac{1}{\alpha-1}\log_2\sum_{c}q(c)^{\alpha}p(c)^{1-\alpha}$ (with
$+\infty$ if $\mathbf q\not\ll\mathbf p$), and
$D_{\infty}(\mathbf q\|\mathbf p)\coloneqq\log_2\max_c\frac{q(c)}{p(c)}$.
For $X,Y\in\Pos{}$ the quantum relative entropy is
$\Dtwo(X\|Y)=\tr[X(\log_2X-\log_2Y)]$ when
$\operatorname{supp}X\subseteq\operatorname{supp}Y$, else $+\infty$.

The Kullback--Leibler divergence of probability vectors is non-negative,
$\sfD(\mathbf q\|\mathbf p)\ge0$, with equality if and only if
$\mathbf q=\mathbf p$ (Gibbs' inequality). If $q(c)>0=p(c)$ for some $c$,
then $\sfD(\mathbf q\|\mathbf p)=+\infty$. Otherwise, with
$S\coloneqq\{c:q(c)>0\}$, the terms outside $S$ vanish by the first
convention and $\log_2$ is strictly concave, so Jensen's inequality with the
weights $q(c)$, $c\in S$, which sum to one, gives
$-\sfD(\mathbf q\|\mathbf p)=\sum_{c\in S}q(c)\log_2\frac{p(c)}{q(c)}
\le\log_2\sum_{c\in S}p(c)\le\log_21=0$. Equality in the first step
forces $p(c)/q(c)$ to be one constant $\gamma$ on $S$, and in the second
$\sum_{c\in S}p(c)=1$; then $\gamma=\gamma\sum_{c\in S}q(c)
=\sum_{c\in S}p(c)=1$, so $\mathbf p=\mathbf q$ on $S$, and $\mathbf p$
vanishes off $S$, its mass on $S$ being one. Conversely
$\sfD(\mathbf q\|\mathbf q)=0$ term by term.
\end{definition}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Used by}\extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/cor:drop-program}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/def:feasible}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/fact:meat}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/frank-wolfe/cor:fo-dropped}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/frank-wolfe/lem:certified-bracket}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/frank-wolfe/lem:fo-khyp}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/lem:objective-homogeneous}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/prop:drop-bound}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/prop:minimal-divergence}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/prop:model-pass-bound}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/prop:optol-nobound}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/prop:value-range}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/thm:accumulated-entropy}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/thm:oracle}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep implemented
\metasep \metalabel{Code}\coderef{https://github.com/fraunhofersg/certiqs-key/blob/v0.1.0/src/certiqs_key/foundations/kernel.py}{certiqs_key.foundations.kernel:divergence_kernel}}

% claim foundations/lem:kernel
\claimsummary{foundations/lem:kernel}{The divergence kernel d(u, v) = u log\ensuremath{_{2}}(u/v), extended to vanishing arguments, is jointly convex, lower semicontinuous and non-increasing in v. These properties keep the objective well defined at support boundaries and let it be composed with concave branch quantities.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/lem:kernel}{Lemma}{lem:kernel}{Extended divergence kernel}
\begin{mainclaim}
\begin{lemma}[Extended divergence kernel]\label{lem:kernel}
Define $d:[0,\infty)\times[0,\infty)\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ by
$d(u,v)\coloneqq u\log_2\frac uv$ for $u,v>0$, $d(0,v)\coloneqq0$ for
$v\ge0$, and $d(u,0)\coloneqq+\infty$ for $u>0$. Then $d$ is jointly
convex and lower semicontinuous, and non-increasing in $v$.
\end{lemma}
\end{mainclaim}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Used by}\extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/cor:drop-program}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/prop:a-neutral}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/prop:drop-bound}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/prop:model-pass-bound}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/thm:convexity}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/thm:oracle}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep implemented
\metasep \metalabel{Code}\coderef{https://github.com/fraunhofersg/certiqs-key/blob/v0.1.0/src/certiqs_key/foundations/kernel.py}{certiqs_key.foundations.kernel:divergence_kernel}
\metasep \metalabel{Oracles}\coderef{https://github.com/fraunhofersg/certiqs-key/blob/v0.1.0/tests/oracles/registry.py}{registry.py}}

\begin{proof}
$d$ is the closed perspective of $g(t)=t\log_2t$ (with $g(0)=0$), i.e.\
$d(u,v)=v\,g(u/v)$ for $v>0$. \emph{Convexity:} let
$(u_i,v_i)$, $i=1,2$, and $\lambda\in(0,1)$, and write
$(u_{\lambda},v_{\lambda})$ for the convex combination. If
$v_1,v_2>0$, then with weights
$\mu_i\coloneqq\lambda_iv_i/v_{\lambda}$ (where
$\lambda_1=\lambda$, $\lambda_2=1-\lambda$; $\mu_1+\mu_2=1$),
\begin{equation*}
  d(u_{\lambda},v_{\lambda})
  =v_{\lambda}\,g\!\Big(\mu_1\tfrac{u_1}{v_1}+\mu_2\tfrac{u_2}{v_2}\Big)
  \le v_{\lambda}\Big[\mu_1g\big(\tfrac{u_1}{v_1}\big)
  +\mu_2g\big(\tfrac{u_2}{v_2}\big)\Big]
  =\lambda d(u_1,v_1)+(1-\lambda)d(u_2,v_2)
\end{equation*}
by convexity of $g$. If, say, $v_2=0$ and $u_2>0$, the right-hand side is
$+\infty$ and the inequality is trivial; if $v_2=0$ and $u_2=0$, then
$(u_{\lambda},v_{\lambda})=\lambda(u_1,v_1)$ and
$d(\lambda u_1,\lambda v_1)=\lambda d(u_1,v_1)$, again consistent.
\emph{Monotonicity in $v$:} for $u>0$, $v\mapsto u\log_2(u/v)$ is
decreasing on $(0,\infty)$ and jumps to $+\infty$ at $v=0$; for $u=0$ it is
constant. \emph{Lower semicontinuity:} at $(u,0)$ with $u>0$, any sequence
$(u_n,v_n)\to(u,0)$ with $v_n>0$ has
$u_n\log_2(u_n/v_n)\to+\infty$; at $(0,v)$ with $v>0$,
$|u_n\log_2(u_n/v_n)|\le u_n|\log_2u_n|+u_n|\log_2v_n|\to0$; at $(0,0)$,
for $v_n\le\frac12$ eventually,
$u_n\log_2(u_n/v_n)\ge u_n\log_2u_n\to0$, so
$\liminf\ge0=d(0,0)$.
\end{proof}

% claim foundations/lem:pinchmono
\claimsummary{foundations/lem:pinchmono}{For \ensuremath{\alpha} \textgreater{} 1, pinching the \ensuremath{\alpha}-th root of a positive semidefinite operator and raising the result to the power \ensuremath{\alpha} never increases the trace, and leaves it unchanged exactly when the operator is block diagonal for the pinching. This bounds the trace-power terms of the MEAT objective.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/lem:pinchmono}{Lemma}{lem:pinchmono}{Pinching lowers the trace power}
\begin{mainclaim}
\begin{lemma}[Pinching lowers the trace power]\label{lem:pinchmono}
Let $\tau\in\Pos{Q}$, let $\cZ$ be a pinching with projectors
$\{Z_j\}_{j=1}^{m}$, and let $\alpha\in(1,\infty)$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pinchmono}
  \tr\!\left[\left(\cZ\big(\tau^{1/\alpha}\big)\right)^{\alpha}\right]
  \;\le\;\tr[\tau],
\end{equation}
with equality if and only if $\cZ(\tau^{1/\alpha})=\tau^{1/\alpha}$,
equivalently iff $\tau$ is block-diagonal for $\{Z_j\}$, equivalently iff
$\cZ(\tau)=\tau$.
\end{lemma}
\end{mainclaim}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Uses}\mref{Def.}{def:pinching}
\metasep \metalabel{Used by}\extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/cor:f-nonpos}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/frank-wolfe/prop:relaxed-set-properties}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/thm:branch-formula}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep implemented
\metasep \metalabel{Code}\coderef{https://github.com/fraunhofersg/certiqs-key/blob/v0.1.0/src/certiqs_key/meat_core/objective/branch.py}{certiqs_key.meat_core.objective.branch:trace_power_pinched}
\metasep \metalabel{Oracles}\coderef{https://github.com/fraunhofersg/certiqs-key/blob/v0.1.0/tests/oracles/registry.py}{registry.py}}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Step 1 (pinching as a unitary mixture).} With
$\zeta\coloneqq e^{2\pi i/m}$ and the unitaries
$U_k\coloneqq\sum_{j=1}^{m}\zeta^{jk}Z_j$, $k\in\{0,\dots,m-1\}$,
\eqref{eq:pinch-unitary-mixture} of Definition~\ref{def:pinching} gives
$\cZ(X)=\frac1m\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}U_kXU_k^{\dagger}$ for every $X$.

\emph{Step 2 (strict convexity of $A\mapsto\tr[A^{\alpha}]$ on
$\Pos{Q}$).} Two standard facts, proved inline for self-containment. (a)
\emph{Peierls inequality with equality condition:} for convex
$f:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$, any ONB $\{\ket{i}\}$ and $A\in\Pos{Q}$ with
spectral decomposition $A=\sum_j\lambda_j\dyad{a_j}$,
\begin{equation*}
  \bra{i}f(A)\ket{i}
  =\sum_j|\braket{i}{a_j}|^2f(\lambda_j)
  \;\ge\;f\Big(\sum_j|\braket{i}{a_j}|^2\lambda_j\Big)
  =f\big(\bra{i}A\ket{i}\big)
\end{equation*}
by Jensen; summing over $i$ gives
$\tr f(A)\ge\sum_if(\bra{i}A\ket{i})$. If $f$ is strictly convex, equality
for index $i$ forces the distribution $|\braket{i}{a_j}|^2$ to be supported
on a single eigenvalue of $A$, i.e.\ $\ket{i}$ lies in one eigenspace of
$A$; equality for all $i$ forces $\{\ket{i}\}$ to be an eigenbasis of $A$.
(b) \emph{Strict convexity of the trace functional:} let
$f(t)=t^{\alpha}$, strictly convex on $[0,\infty)$ for $\alpha>1$. For
$A,B\in\Pos{Q}$ let $C=\tfrac12(A+B)$ with eigenbasis $\{\ket{i}\}$. Then
\begin{equation*}
  \tr f(C)=\sum_if\big(\bra{i}C\ket{i}\big)
  =\sum_if\Big(\tfrac{\bra iA\ket i+\bra iB\ket i}{2}\Big)
  \le\sum_i\tfrac{f(\bra iA\ket i)+f(\bra iB\ket i)}{2}
  \le\tfrac{\tr f(A)+\tr f(B)}{2},
\end{equation*}
using scalar convexity and then Peierls for $A$ and $B$. By continuity,
midpoint convexity gives convexity. If equality holds throughout, then (by
strict scalar convexity) $\bra iA\ket i=\bra iB\ket i$ for all $i$, and (by
the Peierls equality condition) $\{\ket i\}$ is an eigenbasis of both $A$
and $B$; hence $A$ and $B$ are diagonal in a common basis with equal
diagonals, so $A=B$. Thus $A\mapsto\tr[A^{\alpha}]$ is strictly convex.

\emph{Step 3 (conclusion).} Set $X\coloneqq\tau^{1/\alpha}$. By Steps 1--2
and unitary invariance of the trace functional,
\begin{equation*}
  \tr\big[\cZ(X)^{\alpha}\big]
  =\tr\Big[\Big(\tfrac1m\sum_kU_kXU_k^{\dagger}\Big)^{\alpha}\Big]
  \le\frac1m\sum_k\tr\big[(U_kXU_k^{\dagger})^{\alpha}\big]
  =\tr[X^{\alpha}]=\tr[\tau].
\end{equation*}
For the equality case: a strictly convex functional satisfies the
$m$-point Jensen inequality with equality only if all arguments coincide
(if two differed, replacing them by their midpoint would strictly decrease
the right side while fixing the left, a contradiction). Hence equality in
\eqref{eq:pinchmono} forces $U_kXU_k^{\dagger}=U_0XU_0^{\dagger}=X$ for all
$k$, so $X=\frac1m\sum_kU_kXU_k^{\dagger}=\cZ(X)$, i.e.\
$\tau^{1/\alpha}$ is block-diagonal. Since $\tau=(\tau^{1/\alpha})^{\alpha}$
and functional calculus preserves block-diagonality in both directions,
this is equivalent to $\cZ(\tau)=\tau$. Conversely, if
$\cZ(\tau^{1/\alpha})=\tau^{1/\alpha}$ then
\eqref{eq:pinchmono} holds with equality by direct substitution.
\end{proof}

% claim foundations/fact:pinch-id
\claimsummary{foundations/fact:pinch-id}{For a purified input and a projective key measurement, the fixed-marginal conditional R\'enyi entropy equals a trace-power expression involving only the measured system's marginal. This removes the explicit purifier from the computable branch objective.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/fact:pinch-id}{Fact}{fact:pinch-id}{Pinched trace-power form of the conditional Rényi entropy}
\begin{fact}[Pinched trace-power form of the conditional Rényi entropy]\label{fact:pinch-id}
Let $\rho_{QE}\in\Seq{QE}$ be pure, let $\{Z_j\}_{j=1}^{d}$ be orthogonal
projectors on $Q$ with $\sum_jZ_j=\idon{Q}$, let
$\VZ=\sum_j\ket{j}_{S}\otimes Z_j$ and
$\sigma_{SQE}\coloneqq\VZ\,\rho_{QE}\,\VZ^{\dagger}$, and let
$\cZ(\tau)\coloneqq\sum_jZ_j\tau Z_j$. Then, for $\alpha\in(1,\infty)$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pinch-id}
  \Hsanddown(S|E)_{\sigma_{SE}}
  =\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\log_2
  \tr\!\left[\left(\cZ\big(\rho_Q^{1/\alpha}\big)\right)^{\alpha}\right].
\end{equation}
\emph{Locator note.} The source states no $\alpha$ restriction in the
theorem; the domain $(1,\infty)$ used here lies inside the domain
$(0,1)\cup(1,\infty)$ of its entropy definitions and is the only range any
claim that uses this fact invokes.
\end{fact}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Uses}\mref{Def.}{def:pinching}, \mref{Def.}{def:renyi}
\metasep \metalabel{Used by}\extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/thm:branch-formula}
\metasep published in \cite[{Thm. 8, Eq. (59)}]{kamin2025renyi}
\metasep accepted
\metasep \metalabel{Oracles}\coderef{https://github.com/fraunhofersg/certiqs-key/blob/v0.1.0/tests/oracles/registry.py}{registry.py}}

% claim foundations/fact:concavity
\claimsummary{foundations/fact:concavity}{The pinched trace-power functional is concave on subnormalised states for every parameter in [0, 1]. This is the analytic ingredient behind the convexity of the engine's objective.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/fact:concavity}{Fact}{fact:concavity}{Concavity of the pinched trace-power functional}
\begin{fact}[Concavity of the pinched trace-power functional]\label{fact:concavity}
Let $\cZ$ be a pinching built from a complete family of mutually orthogonal
projectors (Def.~22 of the source) and for $\alpha'\in[0,2]$ let
$Q_{\alpha'}(\rho)\coloneqq
\tr[(\cZ(\rho^{\alpha'}))^{1/\alpha'}]$ (Eq.~(F6) of the source). Then
$\rho\mapsto Q_{\alpha'}(\rho)$ is concave on $\Sleq{Q}$ for
$\alpha'\in[0,1]$.
\end{fact}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Used by}\extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/cor:concavity}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/lem:cone-concavity}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/thm:gradient}
\metasep published in \cite[{App. F.1, Thm. 24}]{kamin2025renyi}
\metasep accepted
\metasep \metalabel{Oracles}\coderef{https://github.com/fraunhofersg/certiqs-key/blob/v0.1.0/tests/oracles/registry.py}{registry.py}}

\section{The round model}\label{group-foundations/def:round-model}
\sectionintro{A run of n rounds is attacked by a sequence of channels, one per round, each delivering the per-round system, with Alice's system too where the adversary supplies it, and carrying Eve's memory forward. A list of operator constraints restricts each round's channel by adjoint conditions, which cut out an \termref{term-attack-set}{attack set}, with a stronger condition for an entry scoped to one factor of a product system. A register of any dimension, such as an adversary's memory, is approximated by compressing it onto a finite-dimensional subspace, at a cost in trace norm that the state's weight outside the subspace bounds and that adds along a sequence of channels (\hyperlink{claim-foundations/lem:register-compression}{Lemma~\ref*{lem:register-compression}}). The \termref{term-round-model}{round model} is stated once for a generic per-round system, and the modules that analyse a protocol instantiate it at their own systems. A family of objects describing a round is round-homogeneous when the same objects describe every round and every round behaves as they describe whatever the other rounds do, so no device has memory across rounds; the modules' round assumptions assert it, or its sameness clause alone where they say so, of their own families.}

% claim foundations/def:round-model
\claimsummary{foundations/def:round-model}{Over n rounds of a per-round system S, an attack sequence is one channel per round from Eve's register to S and her new memory, with Alice's system too when the adversary supplies it. A list of operator constraints cuts out an attack set by adjoint conditions, and so the admissible attack sequences.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/def:round-model}{Definition}{def:round-model}{Round model, attack sequences and attack sets}
\begin{definition}[Round model, attack sequences and attack sets]\label{def:round-model}
Fix a number $n\geq1$ of rounds, a per-round system $S$, Alice's system $A$,
and the instantiating model's source mode: in \exttermref{../transmitter/contract.pdf}{term-trusted-source-mode}{trusted-source mode} Alice
supplies $A$ in every round, and in \exttermref{../transmitter/contract.pdf}{term-untrusted-source-mode}{untrusted-source mode} the adversary
does. Systems, operators and channels follow the conventions of
Definition~\ref{def:pinching}, except that $S$ may be separable of infinite
dimension where the instantiating model declares it so; a channel whose input
or output includes such a system is a normal CPTP map on trace-class
operators. The dimensions are the instantiating model's to declare. We write
$S_j$ and $A_j$ for the copies of $S$ and $A$ in round $j$, and drop the
round index where one round is in view. This is the \termdef{term-round-model}{round model} with
per-round system $S$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item An \termdef{term-attack-sequence}{attack
  sequence} is a family $(\Aev_j)_{j=1}^{n}$ of channels whose output carries
  the systems the adversary supplies in the source mode:
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:round-attack}
    \Aev_j\in
    \begin{cases}
      \mathrm{CPTP}\big(E_{j-1},\ S_j\,E'_j\big),
        & \text{trusted-source mode},\\[0.3ex]
      \mathrm{CPTP}\big(E_{j-1},\ A_j\,S_j\,E'_j\big),
        & \text{untrusted-source mode},
    \end{cases}
  \end{equation}
  where $E_0$ is Eve's initial register, $E'_j$ her outgoing memory, and
  $E_j$ her register after round $j$, which holds $E'_j$ together with what
  the instantiating model hands her in round $j$. In trusted-source mode $A_j$
  is \emph{not} an output of $\Aev_j$: it is supplied by Alice and carried
  into the round as a separate input.
\item Let $S$ be finite-dimensional, and let
  $\CList=\{(\hat O_k,\bowtie_k,c_k)\}_{k=1}^{m}$, $m\geq0$, be a
  finite list of Hermitian operators $\hat O_k$ on $S$, relations
  $\bowtie_k\in\{\preceq,=,\succeq\}$ between operators, and real numbers
  $c_k$. For registers $E',E''$, the \termdef{term-attack-set}{attack
  set} of $\CList$ is
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:round-attset}
    \AttSet_{\CList}(E',\,S E'')\coloneqq
    \Big\{\Aev\in\mathrm{CPTP}(E',S E''):\
    \Aev^{\dagger}\big(\hat O_k\otimes\idon{E''}\big)
    \bowtie_k c_k\,\idon{E'}\ \ \forall k\Big\}
    \qquad\text{(trusted-source mode)},
  \end{equation}
  and, with the constraint operator lifted to the larger supplied system,
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:round-attset-un}
    \AttSet_{\CList}(E',\,A S E'')\coloneqq
    \Big\{\Aev\in\mathrm{CPTP}(E',A S E''):\
    \Aev^{\dagger}\big(\idon{A}\otimes\hat O_k\otimes\idon{E''}\big)
    \bowtie_k c_k\,\idon{E'}\ \ \forall k\Big\}
  \end{equation}
  in untrusted-source mode; the two are distinguished by the output system
  named in the argument. For $\CList=\varnothing$ the condition is empty and
  $\AttSet_{\varnothing}=\mathrm{CPTP}$.
\item Where $S$ is finite-dimensional and $S=\bigotimes_{f\in\mathbb{F}}S_f$
  is a product of factors indexed by a finite ordered set $\mathbb{F}$ (with a
  round index as well, a factor is written $S_{f,j}$), an entry of
  $\CList$ may be \emph{tagged} with a factor $f$; its operator $\hat O_k$ is
  then Hermitian on $S_f$, and the entry $(\hat O_k,\bowtie_k,c_k;f)$
  contributes to the attack set, in place of the condition of
  \eqref{eq:round-attset} or \eqref{eq:round-attset-un}, the condition
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:round-attset-pl}
    \big(\idmap_{R'}\otimes\Aev\big)^{\dagger}
    \Big(X\otimes\big(\hat O_k-c_k\,\idon{S_f}\big)\otimes\idon{E''}\Big)
    \;\bowtie_k\;0
    \qquad\text{for every finite-dimensional }R'\text{ and every }
    X\in\Pos{R'R\,S_{f^c}} ,
  \end{equation}
  as an operator on $R'E'$, where $S_{f^c}$ is the product of the factors
  other than $f$, the tensor factors of the argument are written in the order
  $R'R\,S_{f^c}$, $S_f$, $E''$, and $R$ is $A$ in untrusted-source mode and
  trivial in trusted-source mode. Untagged entries keep their conditions. The
  reference system $R'$ is what carries Alice's retained system in
  trusted-source mode, where $A$ is no output of $\Aev$. With $R'$ trivial and
  $X=\idon{}$, \eqref{eq:round-attset-pl} is the condition of
  \eqref{eq:round-attset} or \eqref{eq:round-attset-un} for the lifted operator
  $\idon{S_{f^c}}\otimes\hat O_k$, because $\Aev^{\dagger}$ is unital; so the
  attack set with tagged entries is contained in the attack set with the same
  entries untagged and their operators lifted.
\item An attack sequence is an \termdef{term-admissible-attack-sequence}{admissible attack sequence} for
  $\CList$, or \emph{$\CList$-admissible}, if $\Aev_j$ lies in the attack set
  of $\CList$ of the source mode, \eqref{eq:round-attset} or
  \eqref{eq:round-attset-un} with the conditions of
  \eqref{eq:round-attset-pl} for tagged entries, with $E'=E_{j-1}$ and
  $E''=E'_j$, for every $j$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Uses}\mref{Def.}{def:pinching}
\metasep \metalabel{Used by}\mref{Def.}{def:round-homogeneity}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/ass:eve-dim}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/def:roundmodel}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/def:attset}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/def:roundmodel}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep accepted}

% claim foundations/def:round-homogeneity
\claimsummary{foundations/def:round-homogeneity}{A per-round family is round-homogeneous when one fixed list of objects describes every round (sameness) and every round behaves as they describe whatever the other rounds do (no memory across rounds). An assumption may assert sameness alone, and must then say so.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/def:round-homogeneity}{Definition}{def:round-homogeneity}{Round homogeneity of a per-round family}
\begin{definition}[Round homogeneity of a per-round family]\label{def:round-homogeneity}
Consider the $n$ rounds of a round model (Definition~\ref{def:round-model}),
and a \termdef{term-per-round-family}{per-round family}: a finite list of objects that a model of the
run declares for a round, such as operators, channels or a declaration. The
family is \termdef{term-round-homogeneous}{round-homogeneous}
if both of the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item \emph{Sameness.} One list of objects, fixed before the run, describes
  every round: for every $j\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ round $j$ is described by the
  same objects. No object of the family depends on the round index or on the
  run.
\item \emph{No memory.} Every round behaves physically as the objects
  describe it, whatever the inputs and the outputs of the other rounds are.
  This excludes memory across rounds, such as detector memory, afterpulsing
  or correlations between a source's emissions in different rounds. It is a
  condition on the rounds, not on the objects, and does not follow from (i).
\end{enumerate}
An assumption may assert (i) alone of its family, and must then say so; an
assumption that calls its family round-homogeneous without saying so asserts
(i) and (ii). Rounds are not averaged: a family that describes the rounds
only on average over the rounds, or up to a per-round variation, does not
satisfy (i), and
per-round variation is not modelled. Round homogeneity constrains the family
and the rounds it describes, not the adversary: an attack sequence of the
round model remains arbitrary and may correlate the rounds.
\end{definition}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Uses}\mref{Def.}{def:round-model}
\metasep \metalabel{Used by}\extref{../protocol-compiler/contract.pdf}{protocol-compiler/ass:rhom}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/ass:round}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/ass:round}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep accepted}

% claim foundations/lem:register-compression
\claimsummary{foundations/lem:register-compression}{Compressing one register of a state onto a finite-dimensional subspace moves the state by at most 2\ensuremath{\surd}\ensuremath{\delta} + \ensuremath{\delta} in trace norm, \ensuremath{\delta} being its weight outside the subspace, whatever the other systems are. The moves add along a sequence of channels, and every channel extends by an identity of any dimension.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/lem:register-compression}{Lemma}{lem:register-compression}{Compressing a register onto a finite-dimensional subspace}
\claimleadin{%
A register of any dimension is approximated by a finite one by compressing
it: the part of a state on a finite-dimensional subspace is kept, and the
weight outside it is moved onto a fixed state of the subspace. The lemma
bounds what that costs in trace norm, with no condition on the other systems,
and adds the costs along a sequence of channels; the compressed register can
then be read as a finite-dimensional one, and channels acting on the other
systems do not see the difference. \xref{meat-core/lem:memory-lift} applies
it to the adversary's registers of a run. The route is that of
\cite[Def.~A.1, Lemma~A.1, Eqs.~(A2)--(A5)]{tupkary2026decoy}, re-derived
here with an explicit bound.
}
\begin{lemma}[Compressing a register onto a finite-dimensional subspace]\label{lem:register-compression}
\emph{Setting.} In this lemma a Hilbert space may have any dimension, finite
or infinite, separable or not, in departure from the convention of
Definition~\ref{def:pinching}, and every system named is of this kind.
$\Tcl{Z}$ is the space of trace-class operators on $\Hs{Z}$ with the trace
norm $\|\cdot\|_1$, and $RM$ is the Hilbert-space tensor product of $R$ and
$M$. A \emph{channel} $\Tcl{Z}\to\Tcl{Z'}$ is a trace-preserving linear map
$\Phi$ that is completely positive: for every $k\ge1$ the map that applies
$\Phi$ to every entry of a $k\times k$ matrix of trace-class operators, which
is $\Tcl{\mathbb{C}^kZ}$, is positive. $\tr_R\colon\Tcl{RM}\to\Tcl{M}$ is the
partial trace, fixed by $\tr[X\tr_R(\sigma)]=\tr[(\idon{R}\otimes X)\sigma]$
for every bounded operator $X$ on $\Hs{M}$, and $\tr_M$ likewise.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.6em]
\item \emph{(compression and inclusion)} Let $M^{\circ}$ be a non-zero
  finite-dimensional subspace of $\Hs{M}$, $V$ its inclusion isometry into
  $\Hs{M}$, $\Pi\coloneqq VV^{\dagger}$ the orthogonal projection onto it,
  $\Pi^{\perp}\coloneqq\idon{M}-\Pi$, and $\psi$ a state on $M^{\circ}$. For
  every system $R$ put, for $\sigma\in\Tcl{RM}$ and
  $\tau\in\Tcl{RM^{\circ}}$,
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:compression}
  \begin{gathered}
    \mathcal{P}_R(\sigma)\coloneqq
      (\idon{R}\otimes V)^{\dagger}\sigma(\idon{R}\otimes V)
      +\tr_M\big[(\idon{R}\otimes\Pi^{\perp})\,\sigma\,
        (\idon{R}\otimes\Pi^{\perp})\big]\otimes\psi ,\\
    \iota_R(\tau)\coloneqq(\idon{R}\otimes V)\,\tau\,(\idon{R}\otimes V)^{\dagger},
  \end{gathered}
  \end{equation}
  and write $\mathcal{P}$ and $\iota$ for the case of a one-dimensional $R$.
  Then $\mathcal{P}_R\colon\Tcl{RM}\to\Tcl{RM^{\circ}}$ and
  $\iota_R\colon\Tcl{RM^{\circ}}\to\Tcl{RM}$ are channels,
  $\mathcal{P}_R\circ\iota_R$ is the identity, $\|\iota_R(\tau)\|_1=\|\tau\|_1$
  for every $\tau$, and $\mathcal{P}_R(x\otimes y)=x\otimes\mathcal{P}(y)$ and
  $\iota_R(x\otimes z)=x\otimes\iota(z)$ for $x\in\Tcl{R}$, $y\in\Tcl{M}$ and
  $z\in\Tcl{M^{\circ}}$; more generally, for $R=R_1R_2$,
  $\mathcal{P}_{R_1R_2}(x\otimes y)=x\otimes\mathcal{P}_{R_2}(y)$ and
  $\iota_{R_1R_2}(x\otimes z)=x\otimes\iota_{R_2}(z)$ for $x\in\Tcl{R_1}$,
  $y\in\Tcl{R_2M}$ and $z\in\Tcl{R_2M^{\circ}}$. The channel
  $\mathcal{C}_R\coloneqq\iota_R\circ\mathcal{P}_R$ on $\Tcl{RM}$ is the
  \emph{compression of $M$ onto $M^{\circ}$}.
\item \emph{(one compression)} For every state $\sigma$ on $RM$, with
  $\delta\coloneqq\tr\big[(\idon{R}\otimes\Pi^{\perp})\sigma\big]$,
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:compression-bound}
    \big\|\mathcal{C}_R(\sigma)-\sigma\big\|_1\;\le\;2\sqrt{\delta}+\delta .
  \end{equation}
  For every state $\sigma$ on $RM$ and every $\eta>0$ there is a non-zero
  finite-dimensional subspace $M^{\circ}$, spanned by finitely many
  eigenvectors of $\tr_R(\sigma)$, at which $\delta\le\eta$.
\item \emph{(a sequence of channels)} Let $Z_0,\dots,Z_m$ be systems, $\omega$
  a state on $Z_0$, $\Phi_k\colon\Tcl{Z_{k-1}}\to\Tcl{Z_k}$ channels for
  $k=1,\dots,m$, and $\mathcal{C}_k$ a channel on $\Tcl{Z_k}$ for
  $k=0,\dots,m$. Put $\sigma_0\coloneqq\omega$ and
  $\sigma_k\coloneqq\Phi_k(\sigma_{k-1})$. Then
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:compression-sequence}
    \big\|\mathcal{C}_m\Phi_m\mathcal{C}_{m-1}\cdots\Phi_1\mathcal{C}_0(\omega)
      -\sigma_m\big\|_1
    \;\le\;\sum_{k=0}^{m}\big\|\mathcal{C}_k(\sigma_k)-\sigma_k\big\|_1 .
  \end{equation}
\item \emph{(maps on different factors)} Let $G\colon\Tcl{R}\to\Tcl{R'}$ and
  $H\colon\Tcl{M}\to\Tcl{M'}$ be linear maps, and let
  $G_M\colon\Tcl{RM}\to\Tcl{R'M}$, $G_{M'}\colon\Tcl{RM'}\to\Tcl{R'M'}$,
  $H_R\colon\Tcl{RM}\to\Tcl{RM'}$ and $H_{R'}\colon\Tcl{R'M}\to\Tcl{R'M'}$ be
  linear maps, bounded in trace norm, with $G_M(x\otimes y)=G(x)\otimes y$,
  $G_{M'}(x\otimes y')=G(x)\otimes y'$, $H_R(x\otimes y)=x\otimes H(y)$ and
  $H_{R'}(x'\otimes y)=x'\otimes H(y)$ for all $x\in\Tcl{R}$,
  $x'\in\Tcl{R'}$, $y\in\Tcl{M}$, $y'\in\Tcl{M'}$. Then
  $H_{R'}\circ G_M=G_{M'}\circ H_R$. In particular, with $H=\mathcal{P}$ or
  $H=\iota$, whose extensions are $\mathcal{P}_R$, $\mathcal{P}_{R'}$,
  $\iota_R$ and $\iota_{R'}$ by (i),
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:compression-commute}
    \mathcal{P}_{R'}\circ G_M=G_{M^{\circ}}\circ\mathcal{P}_R,
    \qquad
    G_M\circ\iota_R=\iota_{R'}\circ G_{M^{\circ}} .
  \end{equation}
\item \emph{(extension by an identity)} For every channel
  $\Phi\colon\Tcl{Z}\to\Tcl{Z'}$ and every system $K$ there is exactly one
  linear map $\Phi_K\colon\Tcl{ZK}\to\Tcl{Z'K}$, bounded in trace norm, with
  $\Phi_K(x\otimes y)=\Phi(x)\otimes y$ for all $x\in\Tcl{Z}$ and
  $y\in\Tcl{K}$; it is a channel, written $\Phi\otimes\idmap_K$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Used by}\extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/lem:honest-attacks}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/lem:memory-lift}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep accepted}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Idea.} Each map of (i) is built from conjugations, a partial trace and
the appending of a state. For (ii), the projected state differs from the
state by terms that the weight outside the subspace controls, vector by
vector in a spectral decomposition. Part (iii) is a telescoping sum, every
channel contracting the trace norm of a Hermitian operator, and (iv) holds on
product operators, which span a dense subspace. Part (v) builds the extension
from finite-dimensional subspaces of $K$, as the limit along which part (ii)
lets the state be compressed.

\emph{Step 1 (two facts on channels).} A positive trace-preserving linear map
$\Phi$ satisfies $\|\Phi(Z)\|_1\le\|Z\|_1$ for every Hermitian trace-class
$Z$, and a positive linear map $\Phi$ with $\tr\Phi(Z)\le\tr Z$ for $Z\succeq0$
does too: write $Z=Z^{+}-Z^{-}$ by the spectral decomposition, with positive
$Z^{\pm}$ and $\|Z\|_1=\tr Z^{+}+\tr Z^{-}$; then
$\|\Phi(Z)\|_1\le\|\Phi(Z^{+})\|_1+\|\Phi(Z^{-})\|_1
=\tr\Phi(Z^{+})+\tr\Phi(Z^{-})\le\|Z\|_1$, a positive trace-class operator
having trace norm equal to its trace. Such a map is bounded in trace norm:
every $\tau$ is $H_1+iH_2$ with the Hermitian
$H_1=\tfrac12(\tau+\tau^{\dagger})$ and $H_2=\tfrac1{2i}(\tau-\tau^{\dagger})$,
each of trace norm at most $\|\tau\|_1$, so $\|\Phi(\tau)\|_1\le2\|\tau\|_1$.

\emph{Step 2 (part (i)).} A conjugation $\sigma\mapsto B\sigma B^{\dagger}$ by a
bounded operator is completely positive: applied entrywise to a
$k\times k$ matrix it is the conjugation by $\idon{\mathbb{C}^k}\otimes B$. The
partial trace is completely positive, applied entrywise being the partial
trace on $\mathbb{C}^kRM$; appending the state $\psi$, $Y\mapsto Y\otimes\psi$,
is completely positive; and sums and compositions of completely positive maps
are. So $\mathcal{P}_R$ and $\iota_R$ are completely positive. Trace: for
trace-class $\sigma$ and bounded $B$, $\tr[B^{\dagger}\sigma B]=\tr[\sigma
BB^{\dagger}]$, so
$\tr\mathcal{P}_R(\sigma)=\tr[(\idon{R}\otimes\Pi)\sigma]
+\tr[(\idon{R}\otimes\Pi^{\perp})\sigma]=\tr\sigma$, and
$\tr\iota_R(\tau)=\tr[\tau(\idon{R}\otimes V^{\dagger}V)]=\tr\tau$ since $V$ is an
isometry. $\mathcal{P}_R\circ\iota_R$ is the identity because
$(\idon{R}\otimes V)^{\dagger}(\idon{R}\otimes V)=\idon{RM^{\circ}}$ and
$\Pi^{\perp}V=0$, which makes the second term of $\mathcal{P}_R$ vanish on
$\iota_R(\tau)$. For an isometry $W$, $|W\tau W^{\dagger}|=W|\tau|W^{\dagger}$,
since $W|\tau|W^{\dagger}$ is positive with square
$W\tau^{\dagger}\tau W^{\dagger}=(W\tau W^{\dagger})^{\dagger}(W\tau W^{\dagger})$;
taking traces, $\|W\tau W^{\dagger}\|_1=\|\tau\|_1$, which is the claim for
$W=\idon{R}\otimes V$. On products,
$(\idon{R}\otimes V)^{\dagger}(x\otimes y)(\idon{R}\otimes V)=x\otimes
V^{\dagger}yV$ and
$\tr_M[(\idon{R}\otimes\Pi^{\perp})(x\otimes y)(\idon{R}\otimes\Pi^{\perp})]
=\tr[\Pi^{\perp}y\Pi^{\perp}]\,x$, which together give
$x\otimes\mathcal{P}(y)$; the product form of $\iota_R$ is the same
computation. For $R=R_1R_2$ and $x\in\Tcl{R_1}$, $y\in\Tcl{R_2M}$, the
operators $\idon{R_1R_2}\otimes V$ and $\idon{R_1R_2}\otimes\Pi^{\perp}$ are
$\idon{R_1}\otimes(\idon{R_2}\otimes V)$ and
$\idon{R_1}\otimes(\idon{R_2}\otimes\Pi^{\perp})$, so the conjugations act on
$x\otimes y$ as $x$ tensored with the conjugations of $y$, and the partial
trace over $M$ of $x\otimes Y$ is $x\otimes\tr_M Y$ for $Y$ on $R_2M$, by its
defining property tested on products; together they give
$x\otimes\mathcal{P}_{R_2}(y)$, and likewise for $\iota$.

\emph{Step 3 (part (ii)).} Write $P\coloneqq\idon{R}\otimes\Pi$ and
$Q\coloneqq\idon{R}\otimes\Pi^{\perp}$, so that $\delta=\tr[Q\sigma]$ and, by
\eqref{eq:compression},
\begin{equation*}
  \mathcal{C}_R(\sigma)-\sigma
  =\big(P\sigma P-\sigma\big)
  +\tr_M\big[Q\sigma Q\big]\otimes V\psi V^{\dagger} .
\end{equation*}
The second term is positive, being the partial trace of the positive
$Q\sigma Q$ tensored with a state, so its trace norm is its trace,
$\tr[Q\sigma Q]=\tr[Q\sigma]=\delta$. For the first, let
$\sigma=\sum_l\mu_l\dyad{w_l}$ be a spectral decomposition, with
$\mu_l\ge0$, $\sum_l\mu_l=1$ and orthonormal $w_l$, a series converging in
trace norm; the conjugation by $P$ is bounded in trace norm, so
$P\sigma P-\sigma=\sum_l\mu_l\big(\dyad{Pw_l}-\dyad{w_l}\big)$. Since
$w=Pw+Qw$,
$\dyad{Pw}-\dyad{w}=-\ketbra{Qw}{w}-\ketbra{Pw}{Qw}$, and a rank-one operator
$\ketbra{a}{b}$ has trace norm $\|a\|\,\|b\|$, so for a unit vector $w$
the trace norm of this difference is at most $2\|Qw\|$. Hence, by the
Cauchy--Schwarz inequality for the weights $\mu_l$,
\begin{equation*}
  \|P\sigma P-\sigma\|_1\le2\sum_l\mu_l\|Qw_l\|
  \le2\Big(\sum_l\mu_l\|Qw_l\|^2\Big)^{1/2}
  =2\Big(\sum_l\mu_l\bra{w_l}Q\ket{w_l}\Big)^{1/2}
  =2\sqrt{\tr[Q\sigma]}=2\sqrt{\delta},
\end{equation*}
using $\|Qw\|^2=\bra{w}Q\ket{w}$ for the projection $Q$. The triangle
inequality gives \eqref{eq:compression-bound}. For the second sentence, the
partial trace $\sigma_M\coloneqq\tr_R(\sigma)$ is a positive trace-class
operator of trace one, with a spectral decomposition
$\sigma_M=\sum_l\lambda_l\dyad{e_l}$, finite or countable, with $\lambda_l>0$,
$\sum_l\lambda_l=1$ and orthonormal $e_l$, and it has at least one term. By
the defining property of the partial trace,
$\delta=\tr[(\idon{R}\otimes\Pi^{\perp})\sigma]=\tr[\Pi^{\perp}\sigma_M]$. At
$M^{\circ}=\mathrm{span}\{e_1,\dots,e_d\}$, with $d$ at most the number of
terms, $\Pi^{\perp}e_l=0$ for $l\le d$ and $\Pi^{\perp}e_l=e_l$ for $l>d$, so
$\delta=\sum_{l>d}\lambda_l$, the tail of a convergent series of positive
terms; it is at most $\eta$ for $d$ large enough, and zero once $d$ reaches a
finite number of terms.

\emph{Step 4 (part (iii)).} For $k=0,\dots,m$ let
$\mathcal{W}_k\coloneqq\mathcal{C}_m\Phi_m\cdots\mathcal{C}_{k+1}\Phi_{k+1}$,
the identity for $k=m$, and put
$\chi_k\coloneqq\mathcal{W}_k\mathcal{C}_k(\sigma_k)$ and
$\chi_{m+1}\coloneqq\sigma_m$. Then $\chi_0$ is the first state in
\eqref{eq:compression-sequence}, and for $k<m$,
$\chi_{k+1}=\mathcal{W}_{k+1}\mathcal{C}_{k+1}\Phi_{k+1}(\sigma_k)
=\mathcal{W}_k(\sigma_k)$, so that
$\chi_k-\chi_{k+1}=\mathcal{W}_k\big(\mathcal{C}_k(\sigma_k)-\sigma_k\big)$
for every $k\le m$, the case $k=m$ reading
$\mathcal{C}_m(\sigma_m)-\sigma_m$. Each $\mathcal{W}_k$ is a channel and
$\mathcal{C}_k(\sigma_k)-\sigma_k$ is Hermitian, so by Step~1 its image has
trace norm at most $\|\mathcal{C}_k(\sigma_k)-\sigma_k\|_1$. Summing
$\chi_0-\chi_{m+1}=\sum_{k=0}^{m}(\chi_k-\chi_{k+1})$ and applying the
triangle inequality gives \eqref{eq:compression-sequence}.

\emph{Step 5 (part (iv)).} The two composites $H_{R'}\circ G_M$ and
$G_{M'}\circ H_R$ are linear and bounded in trace norm, as compositions of
bounded maps, a channel being bounded by
Step~1. On a product $x\otimes y$,
$H_{R'}G_M(x\otimes y)=H_{R'}(G(x)\otimes y)=G(x)\otimes H(y)
=G_{M'}(x\otimes H(y))=G_{M'}H_R(x\otimes y)$.
Products span a trace-norm dense subspace of $\Tcl{RM}$: finite-rank operators are dense, by truncating the
singular value decomposition $\tau=\sum_ls_l\ketbra{u_l}{v_l}$, whose tail
beyond $L$ terms has trace norm at most $\sum_{l>L}s_l$, with
$\sum_ls_l=\|\tau\|_1$; a rank-one $\ketbra{a}{b}$ is the trace-norm limit of
$\ketbra{a_t}{b_t}$ for finite sums $a_t\to a$ and $b_t\to b$ of product
vectors, which are dense in the tensor product, since
$\|\ketbra{a}{b}-\ketbra{a_t}{b_t}\|_1\le\|a-a_t\|\,\|b\|+\|a_t\|\,\|b-b_t\|$;
and $\ketbra{\sum_s\alpha_s\otimes\beta_s}{\sum_t\gamma_t\otimes\delta_t}
=\sum_{s,t}\ketbra{\alpha_s}{\gamma_t}\otimes\ketbra{\beta_s}{\delta_t}$ is a
finite sum of products. Two bounded linear maps that agree on a set spanning
a dense subspace agree everywhere. For $H=\mathcal{P}$ and $H=\iota$ the
maps $\mathcal{P}_R$, $\mathcal{P}_{R'}$, $\iota_R$ and $\iota_{R'}$ are
channels with the product forms of (i), so \eqref{eq:compression-commute} is
the general identity at these maps.

\emph{Step 6 (part (v)).} For a finite-dimensional subspace $K_0$ of
$\Hs{K}$, with inclusion isometry $W_0$ and $P_0\coloneqq\idon{Z}\otimes
W_0W_0^{\dagger}$, let $\Phi\otimes\idmap_{K_0}$ be the map that applies
$\Phi$ to every entry of an operator on $ZK_0$ written as a matrix in a basis
of $K_0$; it is a channel by complete positivity, and it acts on products as
$\Phi(x)\otimes y$, which determines it, since products span $\Tcl{ZK_0}$.
Put $F_0(\tau)\coloneqq(\idon{Z'}\otimes W_0)\,(\Phi\otimes\idmap_{K_0})
\big((\idon{Z}\otimes W_0)^{\dagger}\tau(\idon{Z}\otimes W_0)\big)\,
(\idon{Z'}\otimes W_0)^{\dagger}$, a composite of channels and a
conjugation, so $\|F_0(\tau)\|_1\le2\|\tau\|_1$ by Step~1. For
$K_0\subseteq K_1$, writing the matrices in a basis of $K_1$ that extends one
of $K_0$ shows $F_0(\tau)=F_1(P_0\tau P_0)$, and $F_1(\tau)=F_1(P_1\tau P_1)$,
so
\begin{equation*}
  \|F_1(\tau)-F_0(\tau)\|_1\le2\|P_1\tau P_1-P_0\tau P_0\|_1
  \le2\|P_1\tau P_1-\tau\|_1+2\|\tau-P_0\tau P_0\|_1 .
\end{equation*}
For a positive $\tau$, the estimate of Step~3, read for $\tau/\tr\tau$, gives
$\|\tau-P_0\tau P_0\|_1\le2\big(\tr\tau\cdot
\tr[(\idon{Z}\otimes(\idon{K}-W_0W_0^{\dagger}))\tau]\big)^{1/2}$, and the last
trace is $\tr[(\idon{K}-W_0W_0^{\dagger})\tr_Z\tau]$, which does not increase
as $K_0$ grows and is below any $\eta>0$ once $K_0$ contains finitely many
eigenvectors of $\tr_Z\tau$ (Step~3). A general $\tau$ is a combination of
four positive ones (Step~1). So, along the finite-dimensional subspaces of
$\Hs{K}$ ordered by inclusion, $F_0(\tau)$ is a Cauchy net in the complete
space $\Tcl{Z'K}$; let $\Phi_K(\tau)$ be its limit. $\Phi_K$ is linear, with
$\|\Phi_K(\tau)\|_1\le2\|\tau\|_1$. For $y$ of finite rank with range and
support in $K_0$, $F_1(x\otimes y)=\Phi(x)\otimes y$ for every $K_1\supseteq
K_0$, so $\Phi_K(x\otimes y)=\Phi(x)\otimes y$; both sides are continuous in
$y$, and finite-rank operators are dense (Step~5), so this holds for every
$y$. It is unique because products span a dense subspace (Step~5). Trace:
$\tr F_0(\tau)=\tr[P_0\tau]\to\tr\tau$. Complete positivity: for $k\ge1$,
applying $F_0$ to every entry of a positive $k\times k$ matrix $\omega$ of
trace-class operators conjugates $\omega$ by $\idon{\mathbb{C}^k}\otimes
\idon{Z}\otimes W_0^{\dagger}$, applies $\Phi$ to every entry of a matrix of
size $k\dim K_0$, which is positive, and conjugates back, so the result is
positive; entrywise, these converge in trace norm to $\Phi_K$ applied to every
entry, and a trace-norm limit of positive operators is positive.
\end{proof}

\section{Binary64 numbers and exact sums}\label{group-foundations/def:binary64}
\sectionintro{\termref{term-declared-value}{Declared values} are \termref{term-binary64-numbers}{binary64 numbers}, read as the dyadic rationals they are. A sum of them is accumulated left to right in a \termref{term-declared-order}{declared order}, and it \termref{term-rounds-nowhere}{rounds nowhere} when every binary64 addition is exact. The main result, \hyperlink{claim-foundations/lem:exact-accumulation}{Lemma~\ref*{lem:exact-accumulation}}, shows that such a sum is the exact sum, so a predicate on it is a predicate on the declared values. An example shows that the order of accumulation changes the computed sum.}

% claim foundations/def:binary64
\claimsummary{foundations/def:binary64}{A declared value is a binary64 number and denotes exactly the dyadic rational it is, with no exact object behind it. A binary64 addition is exact precisely when the true sum is a binary64 number, and a lattice value at k is an integer multiple of two to the power \ensuremath{-}k of modulus at most one.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/def:binary64}{Definition}{def:binary64}{Binary64 numbers, declared values and dyadic lattices}
\begin{definition}[Binary64 numbers, declared values and dyadic lattices]\label{def:binary64}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item Let $\mathbb{B}$ be the set of real numbers $m\,2^{q}$ with
  $m,q\in\mathbb{Z}$, $|m|<2^{53}$ and $-1074\le q\le971$, and let
  $\mathbb{B}_{\mathbb{C}}\coloneqq\{x+iy:\ x,y\in\mathbb{B}\}$. The elements
  of $\mathbb{B}$ are the \termdef{term-binary64-numbers}{binary64 numbers}, the finite values of the
  IEEE~754 binary64 format. Every binary64 number is a dyadic rational, an
  element of $\mathbb{Z}[\tfrac12]$.
\item For a real number $x$ with $|x|<2^{1024}-2^{970}$, $\mathrm{fl}(x)$ is
  $x$ rounded to the nearest element of $\mathbb{B}$, a tie going to the
  element whose $m$ is even in its representation of (i) with the least $q$.
  For $|x|\ge2^{1024}-2^{970}$, $\mathrm{fl}(x)\coloneqq+\infty$ if $x>0$ and
  $-\infty$ if $x<0$; the threshold is the midpoint between the largest
  element $(2^{53}-1)\,2^{971}$ of $\mathbb{B}$ and $2^{1024}$, which is where
  IEEE~754 rounding to nearest overflows. Further,
  $\mathrm{fl}(\pm\infty+y)\coloneqq\pm\infty$ for $y\in\mathbb{B}$. The
  \termdef{term-binary64-sum}{binary64 sum} of $a$
  and $b$ is $\mathrm{fl}(a+b)$. On
  $\mathbb{B}_{\mathbb{C}}$, and on matrices over it, $\mathrm{fl}$ acts on the
  real and on the imaginary part of every entry separately. Two properties of
  $\mathrm{fl}$ are all that is used of it: on real input its value lies in
  $\mathbb{B}\cup\{\pm\infty\}$, and $\mathrm{fl}(x)=x$ for $x\in\mathbb{B}$.
  The binary64 sum of $a$ and $b$ is \emph{exact} when it equals $a+b$; by
  those two properties it is exact if and only if the real and the imaginary
  part of every entry of $a+b$ lie in $\mathbb{B}$.
\item A \termdef{term-declared-value}{declared value} is a binary64
  number stated as a datum. It
  denotes that dyadic rational and nothing else: there is no exact object
  behind it of which it is an approximation, and every predicate stated of
  declared values is a predicate of those rationals. A declared complex value
  is an element of $\mathbb{B}_{\mathbb{C}}$, and a declared matrix is a
  matrix of declared complex values.
\item A \termdef{term-lattice-exponent}{lattice exponent} is an integer
  $k$ with $1\le k\le53$. A real number $x$ is a \termdef{term-lattice-value}{lattice value} at $k$ when
  $2^{k}x\in\mathbb{Z}$ and
  $|x|\le1$; a complex number, or a matrix, is one when the real and the
  imaginary part of every entry are.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Used by}\mref{Lem.}{lem:binary64-lattice}, \mref{Def.}{def:declared-order}, \mref{Lem.}{lem:exact-accumulation}, \mref{Rem.}{rem:summation-order}, \mref{Def.}{def:declared-data}, \mref{Def.}{def:exact-admissibility}, \mref{Rem.}{rem:computed-completeness}, \mref{Def.}{def:tolerance}, \mref{Def.}{def:exact-reference}, \mref{Def.}{def:snap}, \mref{Req.}{req:snap-reference}, \mref{Req.}{req:declared-lattice}, \mref{Req.}{req:rounding-direction}, \mref{Req.}{req:exact-island}, \extref{../protocol-compiler/contract.pdf}{protocol-compiler/def:exact}, \extref{../protocol-compiler/contract.pdf}{protocol-compiler/lem:weighted-factor}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/def:complex-enclosure}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/def:exact-route}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/detector-imperfections/cor:exact-dark-composed}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/req:exact-route-decision}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/thm:exact-and-evaluated}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/def:exactadm}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep implemented
\metasep \metalabel{Code}\coderef{https://github.com/fraunhofersg/certiqs-key/blob/v0.1.0/src/certiqs_key/foundations/exact.py}{certiqs_key.foundations.exact:scalar_is_binary64}}

% claim foundations/lem:binary64-lattice
\claimsummary{foundations/lem:binary64-lattice}{Every lattice value at an exponent k \ensuremath{\le} 53 is a binary64 number, and between two consecutive powers of two the binary64 numbers are the multiples of one power of two, in [1/2, 1) those of two to the power \ensuremath{-}53. Representability of a declared entry is therefore a divisibility condition.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/lem:binary64-lattice}{Lemma}{lem:binary64-lattice}{Binary64 numbers on dyadic lattices}
\begin{lemma}[Binary64 numbers on dyadic lattices]\label{lem:binary64-lattice}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item For every lattice exponent $k$, every real lattice value at $k$ is a
  binary64 number, and every complex lattice value at $k$ lies in
  $\mathbb{B}_{\mathbb{C}}$.
\item For every integer $e$ with $-1022\le e\le1023$,
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:binade}
    \mathbb{B}\cap\big[2^{e},2^{e+1}\big)
    \;=\;2^{e-52}\,\mathbb{Z}\cap\big[2^{e},2^{e+1}\big).
  \end{equation}
  In particular the binary64 numbers in $[\tfrac12,1)$ are the multiples of
  $2^{-53}$ in that interval, and those in $[1,2)$ are the multiples of
  $2^{-52}$ in it.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Uses}\mref{Def.}{def:binary64}
\metasep \metalabel{Used by}\mref{Rem.}{rem:summation-order}, \mref{Rem.}{rem:computed-completeness}, \mref{Req.}{req:declared-lattice}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/def:exactadm}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep accepted}

\begin{proof}
(i) Let $x$ be a real lattice value at $k$ (Definition~\ref{def:binary64}\,(iv))
and write $x=n\,2^{-k}$ with $n\in\mathbb{Z}$; then
$|n|=2^{k}|x|\le2^{k}\le2^{53}$. If $|n|<2^{53}$, then $x=n\,2^{q}$ with
$q=-k\in[-53,-1]\subseteq[-1074,971]$, so $x\in\mathbb{B}$ by
Definition~\ref{def:binary64}\,(i). Otherwise $|n|=2^{53}$, which forces
$k=53$ and $|x|=1$, and $x=(\pm1)\,2^{0}\in\mathbb{B}$. A complex lattice value
has its real and imaginary parts on the lattice, hence in $\mathbb{B}$.

(ii) Let $x=n\,2^{e-52}$ with $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $2^{e}\le x<2^{e+1}$. Then
$2^{52}\le n<2^{53}$, and $q\coloneqq e-52$ satisfies $-1074\le q\le971$
because $-1022\le e\le1023$; so $x\in\mathbb{B}$. Conversely, let
$x=m\,2^{q}\in\mathbb{B}$, as in Definition~\ref{def:binary64}\,(i), with
$2^{e}\le x<2^{e+1}$. Then $m>0$, and $m<2^{53}$ gives
$2^{q}=x/m>2^{e}\,2^{-53}$, so the integer $q$ satisfies $q>e-53$, that is
$q\ge e-52$. Hence $x=\big(m\,2^{q-e+52}\big)\,2^{e-52}$ with
$m\,2^{q-e+52}\in\mathbb{Z}$, which proves \eqref{eq:binade}. The two
particular cases are $e=-1$ and $e=0$.
\end{proof}

% claim foundations/def:declared-order
\claimsummary{foundations/def:declared-order}{A sum of declared values is accumulated left to right in a declared order, and it rounds nowhere when every one of its binary64 additions is exact. Binary64 addition is not associative, so the order is part of the datum.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/def:declared-order}{Definition}{def:declared-order}{Sums in a declared order and sums that round nowhere}
\claimleadin{%
In exact arithmetic the order in which a finite sum is accumulated is
immaterial. Binary64 addition is not associative, so a sum that a predicate
reads comes with its order, and the order is part of the datum
(Remark~\ref{rem:summation-order}).
}
\begin{definition}[Sums in a declared order and sums that round nowhere]\label{def:declared-order}
Let $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$, $n\ge1$, be a finite sequence of elements of
$\mathbb{B}_{\mathbb{C}}$, or of matrices of one shape over
$\mathbb{B}_{\mathbb{C}}$ (Definition~\ref{def:binary64}\,(i)): declared values
and declared matrices (Definition~\ref{def:binary64}\,(iii)), or the computed
inner sums of a sum of sums below. Its
\termdef{term-sequential-sum}{sequential sum} is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:seqsum}
  S_0\coloneqq0,\qquad S_i\coloneqq S_{i-1}+x_i\quad(1\le i\le n),
\end{equation}
and its \termdef{term-computed-sequential-sum}{computed sequential sum} is $\hat S_0\coloneqq0$,
$\hat S_i\coloneqq\mathrm{fl}(\hat S_{i-1}+x_i)$ for $1\le i\le n$
(Definition~\ref{def:binary64}\,(ii)), formed left to right, entrywise, with no
re-ordering and no re-association. The accumulation \termdef{term-rounds-nowhere}{rounds nowhere}
when
every one of its $n$ binary64 additions is exact: for every $1\le i\le n$, every
entry of $\hat S_{i-1}$ is finite and $\hat S_i=\hat S_{i-1}+x_i$.

A \termdef{term-declared-order}{declared order} on a finite alphabet $J$ is a total order
$j_1\prec j_2\prec\dots\prec j_{|J|}$ on $J$, fixed together with $J$. For a
family $\{a_j\}_{j\in J}$ of declared values, or of declared matrices of one
shape, the \termdef{term-sum-in-the-declared-order}{sum in the declared order} is the sequential
sum of
$(a_{j_1},\dots,a_{j_{|J|}})$, and the family's sum rounds nowhere when that
accumulation does. The trace of a declared $d\times d$ matrix $X$ is
accumulated as the sequential sum of $(X_{11},X_{22},\dots,X_{dd})$, in
increasing row index. A sum of such sums over an alphabet with a declared order
rounds nowhere when every inner accumulation rounds nowhere and the sequential
sum, in that order, of the computed inner sums rounds nowhere; that sequential
sum is then the computed sum of sums. Each computed inner sum is then over
$\mathbb{B}_{\mathbb{C}}$: its last addition is exact, so it equals a sum of
finite numbers, and it is a value of $\mathrm{fl}$, which lies in
$\mathbb{B}\cup\{\pm\infty\}$ entry by entry and part by part
(Definition~\ref{def:binary64}\,(ii)). The outer sequential sum is therefore
one of the sequences above.
\end{definition}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Uses}\mref{Def.}{def:binary64}
\metasep \metalabel{Used by}\mref{Lem.}{lem:exact-accumulation}, \mref{Rem.}{rem:summation-order}, \mref{Def.}{def:exact-admissibility}, \mref{Def.}{def:snap}, \mref{Req.}{req:boundary-admission}, \mref{Req.}{req:declared-order}, \mref{Req.}{req:exact-emission}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/def:declaration}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep implemented
\metasep \metalabel{Code}\coderef{https://github.com/fraunhofersg/certiqs-key/blob/v0.1.0/src/certiqs_key/foundations/exact.py}{certiqs_key.foundations.exact:sum_in_declared_order}}

% claim foundations/lem:exact-accumulation
\claimsummary{foundations/lem:exact-accumulation}{A sequential sum rounds nowhere exactly when every exact partial sum is a binary64 number, and then the computed sum equals the exact sum at every step. A predicate stated on such a sum is a predicate on the declared values themselves.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/lem:exact-accumulation}{Lemma}{lem:exact-accumulation}{Exactness of a sum that rounds nowhere}
\begin{mainclaim}
\begin{lemma}[Exactness of a sum that rounds nowhere]\label{lem:exact-accumulation}
Let $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ be a finite sequence of elements of
$\mathbb{B}_{\mathbb{C}}$, or of matrices of one shape over
$\mathbb{B}_{\mathbb{C}}$, such as declared values or the computed inner sums
of a sum of sums, with sequential sum $(S_i)_{i=0}^{n}$ and computed
sequential sum $(\hat S_i)_{i=0}^{n}$ (Definition~\ref{def:declared-order}).
The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item the accumulation rounds nowhere;
\item $\hat S_i=S_i$ for every $0\le i\le n$;
\item for every $1\le i\le n$, the real and the imaginary part of every entry
  of $S_i$ are binary64 numbers.
\end{enumerate}
If they hold, the computed sum $\hat S_n$ is the exact sum
$\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i$.
\end{lemma}
\end{mainclaim}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Uses}\mref{Def.}{def:binary64}, \mref{Def.}{def:declared-order}
\metasep \metalabel{Used by}\mref{Rem.}{rem:summation-order}, \mref{Def.}{def:exact-admissibility}, \mref{Rem.}{rem:computed-completeness}, \mref{Req.}{req:boundary-admission}, \extref{../protocol-compiler/contract.pdf}{protocol-compiler/def:exact}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep accepted}

\begin{proof}
The map $\mathrm{fl}$ acts on the real and the imaginary part of every entry
separately (Definition~\ref{def:binary64}\,(ii)), and $S_i$ and $\hat S_i$ are
formed entry by entry, so it suffices to prove the lemma for a sequence of
real numbers $x_i\in\mathbb{B}$.

(a)$\Rightarrow$(b). By induction on $i$: $\hat S_0=0=S_0$, and if
$\hat S_{i-1}=S_{i-1}$, then (a) gives
$\hat S_i=\hat S_{i-1}+x_i=S_{i-1}+x_i=S_i$.

(b)$\Rightarrow$(c). Let $1\le i\le n$. The value
$\hat S_i=\mathrm{fl}(\hat S_{i-1}+x_i)$ lies in $\mathbb{B}\cup\{\pm\infty\}$,
by the first property of $\mathrm{fl}$ where $\hat S_{i-1}$ is finite and by
its definition on $\pm\infty$ otherwise. By (b) it equals the real number
$S_i$, so $S_i\in\mathbb{B}$.

(c)$\Rightarrow$(a). We show by induction on $i$ that $\hat S_i=S_i$ and that
the $i$-th addition is exact. For $i=0$, $\hat S_0=S_0=0$. Let $1\le i\le n$
and $\hat S_{i-1}=S_{i-1}$. Then $\hat S_{i-1}$ is finite, and
$\hat S_{i-1}+x_i=S_i\in\mathbb{B}$ by (c), so the second property of
$\mathrm{fl}$ gives $\hat S_i=\mathrm{fl}(S_i)=S_i=\hat S_{i-1}+x_i$: the
$i$-th addition is exact, and $\hat S_i=S_i$.

Finally, if (b) holds then $\hat S_n=S_n=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i$ by
\eqref{eq:seqsum}.
\end{proof}

% claim foundations/rem:summation-order
\claimsummary{foundations/rem:summation-order}{Two orderings of the same three binary64 numbers have the same exact sum but different computed sums, and only one of them rounds nowhere. A computed sum is therefore a determinate number only once its order is fixed.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/rem:summation-order}{Remark}{rem:summation-order}{Dependence of a computed sum on its order}
\begin{remark}[Dependence of a computed sum on its order]\label{rem:summation-order}
Binary64 addition is not associative, so the computed sequential sum of
Definition~\ref{def:declared-order} depends on the order of its terms. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:binary64-lattice}\,(ii) the binary64 numbers in $[1,2)$ are the
multiples of $2^{-52}$, so $1+2^{-60}$ lies strictly between the adjacent
binary64 numbers $1$ and $1+2^{-52}$ and is nearer to $1$; hence
$\mathrm{fl}(1+2^{-60})=1$ (Definition~\ref{def:binary64}\,(ii)). The
sequence $(1,-1,2^{-60})$ therefore has computed sequential sum
$0,1,0,2^{-60}$, every addition being exact, while $(1,2^{-60},-1)$ has
computed sequential sum $0,1,1,0$, its second addition rounding. The exact sum is $2^{-60}$ in both orders. Only the first
accumulation rounds nowhere, and its computed sum is the exact sum, as
Lemma~\ref{lem:exact-accumulation} guarantees; the second computed sum is
$0$.
\end{remark}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Uses}\mref{Def.}{def:binary64}, \mref{Lem.}{lem:binary64-lattice}, \mref{Def.}{def:declared-order}, \mref{Lem.}{lem:exact-accumulation}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep accepted}

\section{Declared data and exact admissibility}\label{group-foundations/def:declared-data}
\sectionintro{\termref{term-declared-data}{Declared data} are what an instance states and what a producer emits as its own declaration, and a consumer reads them across a \termref{term-module-boundary}{module boundary}. An operator is a list of blocks against a \termref{term-sector-map}{sector map} and is block diagonal by construction. The section's main definition, \hyperlink{claim-foundations/def:exact-admissibility}{Definition~\ref*{def:exact-admissibility}}, states the five conditions every module's admission shares, and a counterexample shows why a completeness sum must round nowhere.}

% claim foundations/def:declared-data
\claimsummary{foundations/def:declared-data}{Declared data are what an instance states, a supplier's output included, and what a producer emits as its own declaration. A consumer reads declared data across a module boundary; a point a module computes itself is never declared.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/def:declared-data}{Definition}{def:declared-data}{Declared data and the parties to a module boundary}
\begin{definition}[Declared data and the parties to a module boundary]\label{def:declared-data}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item An \termdef{term-instance}{instance} is the party that fixes one protocol's
  device data, protocol data and run configuration. The data it states are
  \termdef{term-declared-data}{declared data}, and it is their
  \termdef{term-declarer}{declarer}.
\item A module is a \termdef{term-supplier}{supplier} when its own claims decide their
  conditions on the data it reads or emits in floating point, at slacks an
  instance declares to it, rather than exactly. A floating-point evaluation of
  a device model is an example. Its numerical output is not
  declared data until an instance states it as its own declared data, and the
  instance is then its declarer. Numbers of a supplier's output that reach
  another module in a run are declared by the instance that fixed the run:
  those it rounds and states, and those it passes on unchanged, whether in a
  declaration of its own or by handing the supplier's output on untouched.
\item A module other than a supplier that emits numerical data to another
  module as its own declaration, constructed from declared data it read, is a
  \termdef{term-producer}{producer} of those data; they are declared data, and the
  producer is
  their declarer. Declared data that a module passes on unchanged keep their
  declarer, and the module is not their producer. A scalar bound that a
  producer emits and that a consumer has replaced by its rounding to a
  binary64 number, in a direction that the producer's own claims license as
  weakening it, is read, at its replaced value, as its producer's declaration
  of that bound, and keeps its producer as declarer; a set defined by such
  bounds is then declared data by (v).
\item A module other than a supplier that reads declared data is a
  \termdef{term-consumer}{consumer} of
  them. The passage of declared data from their declarer to a consumer is a
  \termdef{term-module-boundary}{module boundary}.
\item A set defined by declared data, such as a feasible set or an acceptance
  set, is declared data. An object that a module computes itself in the course
  of a computation, such as an iterate of an optimiser or the return of an
  oracle, is a \termdef{term-computed-object}{computed object} and is not declared data.
\item Every entry of declared operator data is a \termref{term-declared-value}{declared value}
  (Definition~\ref{def:binary64}\,(iii)).
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Uses}\mref{Def.}{def:binary64}
\metasep \metalabel{Used by}\mref{Def.}{def:tolerance}, \mref{Def.}{def:snap}, \mref{Def.}{def:evaluated-off-snap}, \mref{Def.}{def:exact-island}, \mref{Ass.}{ass:snapped-measurement}, \mref{Req.}{req:boundary-admission}, \mref{Req.}{req:consumer-decides-exactly}, \mref{Req.}{req:declared-order}, \mref{Req.}{req:declared-tolerance}, \mref{Req.}{req:tolerance-scope}, \mref{Req.}{req:norm-conversion}, \mref{Req.}{req:who-snaps}, \mref{Req.}{req:snap-reference}, \mref{Req.}{req:declared-lattice}, \mref{Req.}{req:rounding-direction}, \mref{Req.}{req:exact-emission}, \mref{Req.}{req:exact-island}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep accepted}

% claim foundations/def:sector-map
\claimsummary{foundations/def:sector-map}{A sector map names the blocks of an operator by a block kind and an ordered list of identifiers with dimensions. An operator given as one array per block is block diagonal by construction, and its Hermiticity, positivity and completeness hold block by block.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/def:sector-map}{Definition}{def:sector-map}{Sector maps and block-list operators}
\begin{definition}[Sector maps and block-list operators]\label{def:sector-map}
A \termdef{term-sector-map}{sector map} $\mathfrak{m}$ consists of two
components: a block kind,
which is a label naming what its blocks are, and a finite non-empty set
$\mathsf{S}$ of block identifiers listed in a fixed order, each identifier
$s\in\mathsf{S}$ with a dimension $d_s\ge1$. Two sector maps \emph{agree} when
they have the same block kind and the same identifiers, in the same order, with
the same dimensions. A system of dimension $d$ without a declared sector
decomposition carries the \termdef{term-one-block-map}{one-block map} of dimension
$d$: one
identifier, with dimension $d$, and a block kind and an identifier that are
the same for every such system, so that two one-block maps agree if and only
if their dimensions are equal.

A \termdef{term-block-list}{block list} against
$\mathfrak{m}$ is a list
$X=(X^{(s)})_{s\in\mathsf{S}}$ of complex $d_s\times d_s$ matrices. It denotes
the operator $\bigoplus_{s\in\mathsf{S}}X^{(s)}$ on
$\bigoplus_{s\in\mathsf{S}}\mathbb{C}^{d_s}$, and we identify the two: the list
is the operator, and no entry outside the blocks exists to be written, so a
block list is block diagonal by construction. A family of block lists against
$\mathfrak{m}$ is a family
$\{X_j\}_{j\in J}$ of such lists, $X^{(s)}_j$ being the block $s$ of $X_j$.

Because the direct sum acts block by block, $X=X^{\dagger}$ if and only if
$X^{(s)}=X^{(s)\dagger}$ for every $s$; $X\succeq0$ if and only if
$X^{(s)}\succeq0$ for every $s$, since
$\langle v,Xv\rangle=\sum_s\langle v_s,X^{(s)}v_s\rangle$ for $v=(v_s)_s$; and
$\sum_{j\in J}X_j=c\,\idon{}$ for a scalar $c$ if and only if
$\sum_{j\in J}X^{(s)}_j=c\,\idon{d_s}$ for every $s$.
\end{definition}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Used by}\mref{Def.}{def:exact-admissibility}, \mref{Def.}{def:tolerance}, \mref{Def.}{def:exact-reference}, \mref{Def.}{def:snap}, \mref{Def.}{def:evaluated-off-snap}, \mref{Def.}{def:domination}, \mref{Lem.}{lem:domination}, \mref{Ass.}{ass:snapped-measurement}, \mref{Req.}{req:support-safe-snap}, \mref{Req.}{req:exact-emission}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/thm:choi}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/detector-imperfections/cor:exact-dark-composed}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/detector-imperfections/req:dark-composed-reference}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/thm:enclosed-blocks}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep implemented
\metasep \metalabel{Code}\coderef{https://github.com/fraunhofersg/certiqs-key/blob/v0.1.0/src/certiqs_key/foundations/blocks.py}{certiqs_key.foundations.blocks:SectorStructure}}

% claim foundations/def:exact-admissibility
\claimsummary{foundations/def:exact-admissibility}{A declared operator family is exactly admissible for a sector map with constant c when (T) its own sector map agrees, (H) every block is exactly Hermitian, (P) positive, (C) it sums to c times the identity and (S) its declared-order sum rounds nowhere. Each is a property of the declared numbers.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/def:exact-admissibility}{Definition}{def:exact-admissibility}{Exact admissibility of a declared operator family}
\claimleadin{%
The five conditions (T), (H), (P), (C) and (S) of the definition are the
part that every module's admission of a declared operator family shares. A
module may impose further conditions of its own, such as a declared lattice
or conditions on other declared objects. A
module may also carry the dimension clause of (T) by the type of its family:
where each block is typed as a $d_s\times d_s$ matrix for the dimension $d_s$
of the consumer's block $s$, comparing block kind, identifiers and order is the
whole of (T).
}
\begin{mainclaim}
\begin{definition}[Exact admissibility of a declared operator family]\label{def:exact-admissibility}
Let $\mathfrak{m}$ be a sector map with blocks $s\in\mathsf{S}$ of
dimensions $d_s$ (Definition~\ref{def:sector-map}), let $J$ be a finite
non-empty alphabet with a \termref{term-declared-order}{declared order}, let $c$ be a declared value,
and let
$\{a_j\}_{j\in J}$ be a family of block lists against a sector map
$\mathfrak{m}'$ whose entries are declared values
(Definition~\ref{def:binary64}\,(iii)). The family is
