\termdef{term-exactly-admissible}{exactly admissible} for $\mathfrak{m}$ with constant $c$ when
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=2.6em]
\item[(T)] \emph{(sector map)} $\mathfrak{m}'$ agrees with $\mathfrak{m}$;
\item[(H)] \emph{(Hermiticity)} $a^{(s)}_j=a^{(s)\dagger}_j$ for every
  $j\in J$ and $s\in\mathsf{S}$;
\item[(P)] \emph{(positivity)} $a^{(s)}_j\succeq0$ for every $j\in J$ and
  $s\in\mathsf{S}$;
\item[(C)] \emph{(completeness)} $\sum_{j\in J}a^{(s)}_j=c\,\idon{d_s}$ for
  every $s\in\mathsf{S}$, as an identity of the declared numbers;
\item[(S)] \emph{(the sum \termref{term-rounds-nowhere}{rounds nowhere})} for every
  $s\in\mathsf{S}$, the sum of $\{a^{(s)}_j\}_{j\in J}$ in the declared order
  of $J$ rounds nowhere (Definition~\ref{def:declared-order}).
\end{itemize}
The family is exactly admissible for $\mathfrak{m}$ when it is so with
constant $c=1$; it is then a positive operator-valued measure on
$\bigoplus_{s}\mathbb{C}^{d_s}$, by the block-by-block reading of
Definition~\ref{def:sector-map}. Since the block $s$ of a block list against
$\mathfrak{m}'$ is a square matrix of the dimension $\mathfrak{m}'$ gives $s$,
(T) holds if and only if $\mathfrak{m}'$ has the block kind and the
identifiers of $\mathfrak{m}$, in the same order, and every block $a^{(s)}_j$
is a $d_s\times d_s$ matrix, $J$ being non-empty. A family on a system without a declared sector
decomposition is read against the one-block map of that system's dimension,
and (T) then reduces to the agreement of that dimension with the size of the
family's matrices.

Each condition is a property of the declared values themselves and involves no
threshold and no norm: (T) compares declared labels and dimensions, (H) and (C)
are identities between exactly represented numbers, (P) is a property of
matrices with dyadic entries, and (S) is a property of the binary64 additions
that form the declared-order sum. Under (S) the computed
\termref{term-sum-in-the-declared-order}{sum in the declared order} is the exact sum
(Lemma~\ref{lem:exact-accumulation}), so (C) holds if and only if that
computed sum equals $c\,\idon{d_s}$ on every block.
\end{definition}
\end{mainclaim}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Uses}\mref{Def.}{def:binary64}, \mref{Def.}{def:declared-order}, \mref{Lem.}{lem:exact-accumulation}, \mref{Def.}{def:sector-map}
\metasep \metalabel{Used by}\mref{Rem.}{rem:computed-completeness}, \mref{Def.}{def:snap}, \mref{Def.}{def:exact-island}, \mref{Req.}{req:boundary-admission}, \mref{Req.}{req:snap-reference}, \mref{Req.}{req:support-safe-snap}, \mref{Req.}{req:exact-emission}, \extref{../protocol-compiler/contract.pdf}{protocol-compiler/def:exact}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/def:exactadm}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep implemented (effective: accepted)
\metasep \metalabel{Code}\coderef{https://github.com/fraunhofersg/certiqs-key/blob/v0.1.0/src/certiqs_key/foundations/exact_admission.py}{certiqs_key.foundations.exact_admission:admit_family_exact}}

% claim foundations/rem:computed-completeness
\claimsummary{foundations/rem:computed-completeness}{Three positive binary64 numbers can have computed sum exactly one while their true sum exceeds one. A completeness test on the computed sum alone would admit them, which is why the rounds-nowhere condition belongs to exact admissibility.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/rem:computed-completeness}{Remark}{rem:computed-completeness}{A complete computed sum from an incomplete family}
\begin{remark}[A complete computed sum from an incomplete family]\label{rem:computed-completeness}
Conditions (H) and (P) of Definition~\ref{def:exact-admissibility}, together
with the identity of the \emph{computed} declared-order sum with the identity,
do not imply (C). Take the one-block map of dimension one and the family
$(1,2^{-54},2^{-54})$ in this declared order. Its entries are
\termref{term-binary64-numbers}{binary64 numbers},
Hermitian and positive. By Lemma~\ref{lem:binary64-lattice}\,(ii) the binary64
numbers in $[1,2)$ are the multiples of $2^{-52}$, so $1+2^{-54}$ lies strictly
between the adjacent binary64 numbers $1$ and $1+2^{-52}$ and is nearer to $1$;
hence $\mathrm{fl}(1+2^{-54})=1$ (Definition~\ref{def:binary64}\,(ii)), and
the \termref{term-computed-sequential-sum}{computed sequential sum} is
$0,1,1,1$. The exact sum is $1+2^{-53}\neq1$, so (C) fails and the family is
not a positive operator-valued measure. Condition (S) fails at the second
addition; it is the condition under which the computed sum is the exact sum at
every step (Lemma~\ref{lem:exact-accumulation}).
\end{remark}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Uses}\mref{Def.}{def:binary64}, \mref{Lem.}{lem:binary64-lattice}, \mref{Lem.}{lem:exact-accumulation}, \mref{Def.}{def:exact-admissibility}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep accepted}

\section{The declared tolerance and the snap}\label{group-foundations/def:tolerance}
\sectionintro{An instance declares one tolerance, which bounds the defects it may repair in its own data, measured as entrywise defects of differences and as a floor on the least eigenvalue. \hyperlink{claim-foundations/lem:floor-stricter}{Lemma~\ref*{lem:floor-stricter}} shows that the floor is the stricter of the two, by a factor of the dimension that is attained. A snap replaces a declared family by an \termref{term-exactly-admissible}{exactly admissible} one on the declarer's lattice and records what it changed. A measurement family has a reference, the model it is declared from, known exactly or through rational \termref{term-entrywise-enclosure}{entrywise enclosures}, and on some blocks also through an enclosed factor with an exact core (\hyperlink{claim-foundations/def:factor-enclosure}{Definition~\ref*{def:factor-enclosure}}). Entries known to be zero fix the \termref{term-structural-support}{structural support} of each element, which no snap may enlarge, save the flagged last resort of \hyperlink{claim-foundations/req:support-safe-snap}{Requirement~\ref*{req:support-safe-snap}} (iv); a block is kept where the snap is decided equal to the data it is made from, and moved otherwise. An enclosure entry whose disc contains zero may be recentred at zero and widened, and the reference is unchanged (\hyperlink{claim-foundations/lem:recentred-enclosure}{Lemma~\ref*{lem:recentred-enclosure}}). A declarer may hand the reference beside the snap, and a block whose snapped data nothing the key length rests on reads, save the points and the acceptance data, is \termref{term-evaluated-off-its-snap}{evaluated off its snap} (\hyperlink{claim-foundations/def:evaluated-off-snap}{Definition~\ref*{def:evaluated-off-snap}}).}

% claim foundations/def:tolerance
\claimsummary{foundations/def:tolerance}{The declared tolerance is a binary64 number in [0, 1) that bounds the defects of an instance's own data before they are snapped. A defect of a difference is an entrywise maximum modulus, and positivity is measured by a floor on the least eigenvalue.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/def:tolerance}{Definition}{def:tolerance}{The declared tolerance and the defects it bounds}
\begin{definition}[The declared tolerance and the defects it bounds]\label{def:tolerance}
The \termdef{term-declared-tolerance}{declared tolerance} is a binary64 number
$\tnum$ with
$0\le\tnum<1$, stated by an instance in its run configuration
(Definition~\ref{def:declared-data}). For a complex matrix $Y$ we write
$\mxn{Y}\coloneqq\max_{i,l}|Y_{il}|$ for its \emph{entrywise maximum modulus}.
The \termdef{term-defects}{defects} of data are the entrywise maximum moduli of the
differences
their predicates name:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item the \emph{Hermiticity defect} $\mxn{X-X^{\dagger}}$ of a square matrix
  $X$;
\item the \emph{completeness residue}
  $\max_{s\in\mathsf{S}}\mxn{\sum_{j\in J}a^{(s)}_j-c\,\idon{d_s}}$ of a family of
  \termref{term-block-list}{block lists} $\{a_j\}_{j\in J}$ against a
  \termref{term-sector-map}{sector map} with blocks $s\in\mathsf{S}$
  (Definition~\ref{def:sector-map}), read with a declared constant $c$;
\item the \emph{column residue} $\max_{l}\big|\sum_{i}P_{il}-1\big|$ of a real
  matrix $P$ read as column-stochastic;
\item the \emph{trace residue} $|\tr X-1|$ of a square matrix $X$ read as
  having unit trace, and the \emph{sum residue} $\big|\sum_{x}p_x-1\big|$ of a
  vector $p$ read as a probability vector.
\end{enumerate}
The sums here are exact sums. A square matrix $X$ passes the
\termdef{term-positivity-floor}{positivity floor} at $\tnum$
when
$\lmin\big(\tfrac12(X+X^{\dagger})\big)\ge-\tnum$. Data lie
\termdef{term-within-the-declared-tolerance}{within the declared tolerance} when each of their defects is at most
$\tnum$ and each of their blocks read as positive semidefinite passes the
positivity floor at $\tnum$.
\end{definition}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Uses}\mref{Def.}{def:binary64}, \mref{Def.}{def:declared-data}, \mref{Def.}{def:sector-map}
\metasep \metalabel{Used by}\mref{Def.}{def:snap}, \mref{Def.}{def:exact-island}, \mref{Req.}{req:declared-tolerance}, \mref{Req.}{req:tolerance-scope}, \mref{Req.}{req:norm-conversion}, \mref{Req.}{req:who-snaps}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep accepted}

% claim foundations/lem:floor-stricter
\claimsummary{foundations/lem:floor-stricter}{A Hermitian matrix with least eigenvalue at least \ensuremath{-}\ensuremath{\delta} lies within entrywise distance \ensuremath{\delta} of the positive cone, but entrywise distance \ensuremath{\delta} only guarantees a least eigenvalue of \ensuremath{-}d\ensuremath{\delta} in dimension d, and that factor is attained. The two tests are different quantities and never interchangeable.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/lem:floor-stricter}{Lemma}{lem:floor-stricter}{The positivity floor against entrywise closeness to the cone}
\claimleadin{%
The declared tolerance governs two kinds of test, entrywise defects of
differences and a floor on the least eigenvalue
(Definition~\ref{def:tolerance}). The lemma compares them.
}
\begin{lemma}[The positivity floor against entrywise closeness to the cone]\label{lem:floor-stricter}
Let $d\ge1$ and $\delta\ge0$, and write $\opn{\cdot}$ for the operator norm and
$\mxn{\cdot}$ for the entrywise maximum modulus of complex $d\times d$
matrices.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item $\mxn{Y}\le\opn{Y}\le d\,\mxn{Y}$ for every complex $d\times d$
  matrix $Y$.
\item If $X$ is Hermitian and $\lmin(X)\ge-\delta$, then
  $X+\delta\,\idon{d}\succeq0$ and
  $\mxn{(X+\delta\,\idon{d})-X}=\delta$.
\item If $X$ is Hermitian and $\mxn{X-P}\le\delta$ for some $P\succeq0$, then
  $\lmin(X)\ge-d\delta$. The bound is attained: for the $d\times d$ matrix $E$
  with every entry equal to $1$, the matrices $X\coloneqq-\delta E$ and
  $P\coloneqq0$ satisfy $\mxn{X-P}=\delta$ and $\lmin(X)=-d\delta$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Used by}\mref{Req.}{req:norm-conversion}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep accepted}

\begin{proof}
(i) For standard basis vectors $e_i,e_l$,
$|Y_{il}|=|\langle e_i,Ye_l\rangle|\le\opn{Y}$ by the Cauchy--Schwarz
inequality, which is the first inequality. For a unit vector $v$, the
Cauchy--Schwarz inequality applied to each row gives
\begin{equation*}
  \|Yv\|^{2}=\sum_i\Big|\sum_lY_{il}v_l\Big|^{2}
  \le\sum_i\Big(\sum_l|Y_{il}|^{2}\Big)\Big(\sum_l|v_l|^{2}\Big)
  =\sum_{i,l}|Y_{il}|^{2}\le d^{2}\mxn{Y}^{2},
\end{equation*}
so $\opn{Y}\le d\,\mxn{Y}$.

(ii) The Hermitian matrix $X+\delta\,\idon{d}$ has the eigenvalues of $X$
shifted by $\delta$, which are non-negative, so it is positive semidefinite.
The difference $\delta\,\idon{d}$ has diagonal entries $\delta$ and
off-diagonal entries $0$, so its entrywise maximum modulus is $\delta$.

(iii) $X-P$ is Hermitian, $X$ and $P$ being so. For a unit vector $v$,
\begin{equation*}
  \langle v,Xv\rangle=\langle v,Pv\rangle+\langle v,(X-P)v\rangle
  \ge0-\opn{X-P}\ge-d\,\mxn{X-P}\ge-d\delta,
\end{equation*}
by $P\succeq0$, the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality and (i). Since
$\lmin(X)=\min_{\|v\|=1}\langle v,Xv\rangle$ for Hermitian $X$, this gives
$\lmin(X)\ge-d\delta$. For the example, let $u$ be the unit vector with every
entry $d^{-1/2}$; then $E=d\,uu^{\dagger}$, whose eigenvalues are $d$, on $u$,
and $0$, on the orthogonal complement of $u$. So the least eigenvalue of
$-\delta E$ is $-d\delta$, and every entry of $-\delta E-0$ has modulus
$\delta$.
\end{proof}

% claim foundations/def:exact-reference
\claimsummary{foundations/def:exact-reference}{A reference is the model a measurement family is declared from: Hermitian, positive and complete blocks, each read through an entrywise enclosure, a Gaussian-rational centre with rational entrywise radii. It is exact when every radius is zero, and every decision about it is then on rationals.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/def:exact-reference}{Definition}{def:exact-reference}{Reference of a measurement family, exact or enclosed}
\claimleadin{%
A family declared on a lattice is a family of dyadic rationals; the model it
is declared from need not be one. Photon-number blocks written in the
orthonormal occupation basis carry factors $1/\sqrt{n}$ even when every
parameter of the model is rational. A polarisation analyser whose analysed
state is $\cos\alpha\ket{H}+\sin\alpha\ket{V}$ has on the one-photon block
the entries $\cos^2\alpha$, $\cos\alpha\sin\alpha$ and $\sin^2\alpha$ in the
$H$, $V$ basis, which are all rational exactly when $\cos\alpha=0$ or
$\tan\alpha$ is rational; at $\alpha=\pi/4$ the cosine is irrational and
every entry is $1/2$, while at $\alpha=\pi/8$ the entries are irrational. A decision
about such a model is still a decision on rationals when each of its entries
is known to lie in a rational box around a Gaussian-rational centre, and the
definition reads the model through such boxes. A block of the form
$D^{-1}SD^{-1}$, with $S$ Gaussian-rational and $D$ the diagonal matrix of
square roots of positive rationals, receives one from rational bounds on
those square roots (Lemma~\ref{lem:enclosure-psd}\,(ii)), and an entry known
exactly is enclosed with radius zero. A model whose entries are all Gaussian
rationals is the case in which every radius is zero.
}
\begin{definition}[Reference of a measurement family, exact or enclosed]\label{def:exact-reference}
Let $\mathfrak{m}$ be a \termref{term-sector-map}{sector map} with blocks $s\in\mathsf{S}$ of
dimensions $d_s$ (Definition~\ref{def:sector-map}), let $J$ be a finite
non-empty alphabet with a \termref{term-declared-order}{declared order}, and let $c>0$ be a
\termref{term-declared-value}{declared value} (Definition~\ref{def:binary64}\,(iii)). A
\termdef{term-entrywise-enclosure}{entrywise enclosure} of a complex $d\times d$ matrix
$X$ is a pair $(X_c,r)$ of a Hermitian $d\times d$ matrix $X_c$ with entries
in $\mathbb{Q}(i)=\{x+iy:x,y\in\mathbb{Q}\}$, its \emph{centre}, and
rationals $r_{il}=r_{li}\ge0$, its \emph{radii}, with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:entrywise-enclosure}
  \big|X_{il}-(X_c)_{il}\big|\;\le\;r_{il}\qquad\text{for all }i,l .
\end{equation}
A \termdef{term-reference}{reference} against $\mathfrak{m}$ over $J$
with constant $c$ is a family $G=\{G_j\}_{j\in J}$ of block lists against
$\mathfrak{m}$ whose blocks are Hermitian and positive semidefinite, with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:reference-complete}
  \sum_{j\in J}G^{(s)}_j\;=\;c\,\idon{d_s}\qquad\text{for every }s\in\mathsf{S},
\end{equation}
read together with an entrywise enclosure $\big(C^{(s)}_j,r^{(s)}_j\big)$ of
every block $G^{(s)}_j$. It is an
\termdef{term-exact-reference}{exact reference} when every radius is $0$; then
$G^{(s)}_j=C^{(s)}_j$ has entries in $\mathbb{Q}(i)$, and its Hermiticity,
positive semidefiniteness and completeness are properties of finitely many
Gaussian rationals.

For a Hermitian $d_s\times d_s$ matrix $Y$ with entries in $\mathbb{Q}(i)$,
the pair $\big(C^{(s)}_j-Y,\,r^{(s)}_j\big)$ is an entrywise enclosure of
$G^{(s)}_j-Y$, since the two differences in \eqref{eq:entrywise-enclosure}
are equal. A reference is an object of its own beside a family declared from
it: the entries of the declared family are declared values, and each denotes
exactly the dyadic rational it is (Definition~\ref{def:binary64}\,(iii)).
\end{definition}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Uses}\mref{Def.}{def:binary64}, \mref{Def.}{def:sector-map}
\metasep \metalabel{Used by}\mref{Def.}{def:factor-enclosure}, \mref{Def.}{def:snap}, \mref{Lem.}{lem:recentred-enclosure}, \mref{Def.}{def:evaluated-off-snap}, \mref{Rem.}{rem:noise-floor}, \mref{Def.}{def:exact-island}, \mref{Cor.}{cor:least-eigenvalue-over-enclosure}, \mref{Ass.}{ass:snapped-measurement}, \mref{Req.}{req:declared-tolerance}, \mref{Req.}{req:who-snaps}, \mref{Req.}{req:snap-reference}, \mref{Req.}{req:support-safe-snap}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/frank-wolfe/lem:certified-bracket-enclosed}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/req:companion-admission}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/detector-imperfections/cor:exact-dark-composed}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/detector-imperfections/req:dark-composed-reference}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/detector-imperfections/req:snap-fix}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/lem:enclosure-arithmetic}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/req:rigorous-weight}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/thm:enclosed-blocks}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/thm:exact-and-evaluated}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/thm:exact-blocks}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/cor:reference-companion}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/def:emitnorm}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/wpfss/prop:precomposed-blocks}

% claim foundations/def:factor-enclosure
\claimsummary{foundations/def:factor-enclosure}{A factor enclosure knows a matrix as L W L*, with L* the adjoint of some L in a box of complex matrices around Gaussian-rational centres and W an exact positive diagonal core; its members are those products. A reference may carry one on a block beside the block's entrywise enclosure.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/def:factor-enclosure}{Definition}{def:factor-enclosure}{Factor enclosure of a block}
\claimleadin{%
An entrywise enclosure with positive radii of an element whose rank is below
its dimension, and whose support is spanned by no set of coordinate vectors,
contains the element, whose block on the rows the enclosure does not fix at
zero is singular, so no lower bound on a least eigenvalue over it is positive
and it fixes no rank
(Corollary~\ref{cor:least-eigenvalue-over-enclosure}\,(iv)). The projector of
an ideal analyser at an angle whose projector has irrational entries is such
an element. It is often known in another form: as a sum $\sum_m w_m
c_mc_m^{\dagger}$ over columns $c_m$ computed in an enclosing arithmetic, with
exact positive weights $w_m$, as an element is that compresses a projector
through an isometry. Read through its columns, the element keeps the rank the
columns fix (Corollary~\ref{cor:rank-over-factor-enclosure}). The definition
names that reading; it is an addition to a reference, never a replacement of
its entrywise enclosures.
}
\begin{definition}[Factor enclosure of a block]\label{def:factor-enclosure}
Let $d\ge1$ and $k\ge0$ be integers. A
\termdef{term-matrix-box}{matrix box} of complex
$d\times k$ matrices is a pair $(L_c,t)$ of a $d\times k$ matrix $L_c$ with
entries in $\mathbb{Q}(i)$, its \emph{centre}, and rationals $t_{im}\ge0$,
its \emph{radii}; it \emph{contains} a complex $d\times k$ matrix $L$ when
$|L_{im}-(L_c)_{im}|\le t_{im}$ for all $i,m$. For $k=0$ it contains the one
$d\times0$ matrix.

A
\termdef{term-factor-enclosure}{factor enclosure} of a complex $d\times d$ matrix $X$ is a triple $(L_c,t,W)$ of a
matrix box $(L_c,t)$ of complex $d\times k$ matrices and a diagonal
$k\times k$ matrix $W$ with positive rational diagonal entries, its
\emph{core}, such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:factor-enclosure}
  X\;=\;LWL^{\dagger}\qquad\text{for some }L\text{ that }(L_c,t)\text{ contains}.
\end{equation}
The number $k$ is its \emph{number of columns}, a matrix $L$ that the box
contains is a \emph{factor} of the triple, and the matrices $LWL^{\dagger}$
with $L$ a factor are its \emph{members}, $X$ among them; for $k=0$ the one
member is the zero $d\times d$ matrix. Every member is Hermitian and positive
semidefinite, since $x^{\dagger}LWL^{\dagger}x=\|W^{1/2}L^{\dagger}x\|^{2}$
for every $x\in\mathbb{C}^{d}$.

A \termref{term-reference}{reference} $G$ (Definition~\ref{def:exact-reference}) \emph{carries} a
factor enclosure on a block $G^{(s)}_j$ when it is read, besides the
\termref{term-entrywise-enclosure}{entrywise enclosure} $\big(C^{(s)}_j,r^{(s)}_j\big)$ of that block, with
a factor enclosure of $G^{(s)}_j$; the block then satisfies both
\eqref{eq:entrywise-enclosure} and \eqref{eq:factor-enclosure}.
\end{definition}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Uses}\mref{Def.}{def:exact-reference}
\metasep \metalabel{Used by}\mref{Cor.}{cor:rank-over-factor-enclosure}, \mref{Req.}{req:snap-reference}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/cor:reference-companion-factors}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/frank-wolfe/lem:certified-bracket-enclosed}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/frank-wolfe/req:certified-evaluation}, \extref{../protocol-compiler/contract.pdf}{protocol-compiler/lem:weighted-factor}, \extref{../protocol-compiler/contract.pdf}{protocol-compiler/req:reference-companion-compiled}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/detector-imperfections/req:dark-composed-reference}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/thm:factor-blocks}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/cor:companion-factor-enclosure}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/req:reference-companion}

% claim foundations/def:snap
\claimsummary{foundations/def:snap}{A snap replaces data by lattice data of the same shape that meet their conditions exactly, entries known to be zero fixing each element's structural support. A block of a measurement snap is kept where it is decided equal to the data it is made from, and moved otherwise.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/def:snap}{Definition}{def:snap}{Snapping declared data onto a lattice}
\claimleadin{%
One documented procedure produces the snaps an instance applies to what it
declares; a producer that snaps its own emission does so by the procedure its
own claims state. For an operator family read as a measurement the instance
keeps a block whose \termref{term-reference}{reference} (Definition~\ref{def:exact-reference})
is known exactly and already lies on the lattice, and snaps every other block
by a procedure that stays as close to what it starts from as the rule allows
that every element, row and column the data state to be zero stays zero,
which is what the structural support below records
(Requirement~\ref{req:support-safe-snap}); only where that procedure cannot
restore the conditions of the snap does a flagged last resort mix a uniform
family into the elements. The steps are Requirement~\ref{req:snap-reference}
and the shared numerical code (\href{../../../spec/architecture.md}{\nolinkurl{spec/architecture.md}}). A snap
relates nothing to the model it replaced beyond its displacement; a run that
holds a reference can read the snapped family only to find points,
evaluating the numbers its key length rests on with the reference in its
place (Definition~\ref{def:evaluated-off-snap}), and where it does not, it
rests on the snap (Requirement~\ref{req:snap-reference}\,(iii)).
}
\begin{definition}[Snapping declared data onto a lattice]\label{def:snap}
Let $D$ be data a declarer is about to declare, a producer's exact
construction of what it emits (Definition~\ref{def:declared-data}), or a
\termref{term-reference}{reference} of an operator family (Definition~\ref{def:exact-reference})
--- a family of block lists against a sector map
(Definition~\ref{def:sector-map}) over an alphabet with a declared order, a
matrix or a vector --- read with the conditions its declaration states of it,
and let $k$ be a \termref{term-lattice-exponent}{lattice exponent}
(Definition~\ref{def:binary64}\,(iv)). For a family read as a measurement,
those conditions are exact admissibility with its declared constant
(Definition~\ref{def:exact-admissibility}); every sum they read is read in its
declared order (Definition~\ref{def:declared-order}). A \termdef{term-snap}{snap} of $D$ at
$k$ is data $D'$ of the same shape, over the same alphabet in the same order,
every entry of which is a \termref{term-lattice-value}{lattice value} at $k$, and which satisfy those
conditions exactly. Its \emph{displacement} is the largest entrywise modulus
of $D'-D$, taken over every block of every element
(Definition~\ref{def:tolerance}), with $D$ replaced by its centres where $D$
is a reference.

An entry of $D$ is
\termdef{term-structurally-zero}{structurally zero} when
it is known to be exactly zero, which is the following and nothing else: where
$D$ is given as numbers, an entry that is the number $0$; where $D$ is a
reference, an entry whose centre and radius are both $0$. An entry of a
reference whose centre is $0$ and whose radius is not is not structurally
zero. The
\termdef{term-structural-support}{structural support} of a block
$D^{(s)}_j$ is the set of indices $i$ such that row $i$ or column $i$ of
$D^{(s)}_j$ holds an entry that is not structurally zero. A row, a column or
an element all of whose entries are structurally zero is structurally zero,
and an index lies outside the structural support exactly when both its row
and its column are. For a reference, whose centres are Hermitian and whose
radii are symmetric (Definition~\ref{def:exact-reference}), row $i$ of a block
is structurally zero exactly when column $i$ is.

Where $D$ is an operator family read as a measurement against a sector map
with blocks $s\in\mathsf{S}$, over an alphabet $J$, a block $s$ of a snap
$F=D'$ of $D$ is
\termdef{term-kept}{kept} when
$F^{(s)}_j=D^{(s)}_j$ is decided exactly for every $j\in J$, and
\termdef{term-moved}{moved} otherwise. Here $D$ on block $s$ is the data the snap is made
from: the centres of an \termref{term-exact-reference}{exact reference} of the block where the snap
runs on them, a producer's exact construction, or the data as they stand
where the declarer states them with no model behind them. Where the
declarer computes the data of the block from a model of it and the snap
runs on that evaluation, the data the snap is made from are the model, of
which the evaluation is no exact presentation, so no exact decision equates
the snap with them and the block is moved, even where the snap leaves the
evaluation unchanged. A snap with no moved block changes nothing.

The definition fixes what a snap produces and not how. The displacement is a
record of the move, and it is the whole of what relates $D'$ to $D$ here.
\end{definition}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Uses}\mref{Def.}{def:binary64}, \mref{Def.}{def:declared-order}, \mref{Def.}{def:declared-data}, \mref{Def.}{def:sector-map}, \mref{Def.}{def:exact-admissibility}, \mref{Def.}{def:tolerance}, \mref{Def.}{def:exact-reference}
\metasep \metalabel{Used by}\mref{Lem.}{lem:recentred-enclosure}, \mref{Def.}{def:evaluated-off-snap}, \mref{Def.}{def:exact-island}, \mref{Ass.}{ass:snapped-measurement}, \mref{Req.}{req:declared-tolerance}, \mref{Req.}{req:who-snaps}, \mref{Req.}{req:snap-reference}, \mref{Req.}{req:support-safe-snap}, \mref{Req.}{req:declared-lattice}, \mref{Req.}{req:exact-emission}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/rem:declared-measurement}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/detector-imperfections/req:dark-composed-reference}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/detector-imperfections/req:snap-fix}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/cor:reference-companion}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/def:emitnorm}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/thm:emit}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/wpfss/prop:precomposed-blocks}

% claim foundations/lem:recentred-enclosure
\claimsummary{foundations/lem:recentred-enclosure}{Zeroing every centre entry whose enclosure contains zero, and adding its modulus bound to the radius, gives another entrywise enclosure of the same matrix; a reference so recentred is the same reference. Any enclosure of a Hermitian matrix becomes an entrywise one by averaging.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/lem:recentred-enclosure}{Lemma}{lem:recentred-enclosure}{Zeroing the centres an enclosure cannot tell from zero}
\claimleadin{%
An enclosure whose disc contains zero does not say whether the entry it
encloses is zero. A family evaluated at its centres would then carry, at such
an entry, a number of the order of the radius that the model may not have,
and a support decision taken on the evaluation could see support there that
the model lacks. Setting such a centre to zero, and widening the radius by
what was removed, keeps the enclosure valid; the lemma says so and fixes the
rational bound the widening uses. An enclosure formed by arithmetic on
enclosures, of a matrix known to be Hermitian, need not come with a Hermitian
centre and symmetric radii; part (iv) gives it them, so that it can be
recentred in turn.
}
\begin{technicalclaim}
\begin{lemma}[Zeroing the centres an enclosure cannot tell from zero]\label{lem:recentred-enclosure}
Let $(C,r)$ be an entrywise enclosure of a complex $d\times d$ matrix $X$
(Definition~\ref{def:exact-reference}), and let
\begin{equation*}
  Z\;\coloneqq\;\big\{(i,l):(\operatorname{Re}C_{il})^{2}
     +(\operatorname{Im}C_{il})^{2}\le r_{il}^{2}\big\},
\end{equation*}
the entries whose enclosure contains $0$. Put $C'_{il}\coloneqq0$ and
$r'_{il}\coloneqq r_{il}+|\operatorname{Re}C_{il}|+|\operatorname{Im}C_{il}|$
for $(i,l)\in Z$, and $C'_{il}\coloneqq C_{il}$, $r'_{il}\coloneqq r_{il}$
otherwise. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item $Z$ is decided by comparisons of rationals, and $(C',r')$ is an
  entrywise enclosure of $X$: $C'$ is Hermitian with entries in
  $\mathbb{Q}(i)$, and $r'_{il}=r'_{li}\ge0$ are rationals;
\item $r'_{il}\le(1+\sqrt2)\,r_{il}$ for every $(i,l)$, and $r'_{il}=r_{il}$
  wherever $C_{il}=0$; in particular an entry that is
  \termref{term-structurally-zero}{structurally zero} for $(C,r)$ (Definition~\ref{def:snap}) is so
  for $(C',r')$, and every entry of $Z$ has centre $0$ in $(C',r')$;
\item if $G$ is a \termref{term-reference}{reference} with constant $c$ read with enclosures
  $\big(C^{(s)}_j,r^{(s)}_j\big)$, then $G$ read with the enclosures
  $\big(C'^{(s)}_j,r'^{(s)}_j\big)$ formed by (i) from each is a reference
  with the same constant; it is the same family $G$, and it is an
  \termref{term-exact-reference}{exact reference} exactly when the first is;
\item if $X$ is Hermitian and $(\tilde C,\tilde r)$ is any pair of a complex
  $d\times d$ matrix $\tilde C$ with entries in $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ and rationals
  $\tilde r_{il}\ge0$ with $|X_{il}-\tilde C_{il}|\le\tilde r_{il}$ for all
  $i,l$, Hermitian or symmetric or not, then
  $\big(\tfrac12(\tilde C+\tilde C^{\dagger}),\tfrac12(\tilde r+\tilde r^{\mathsf T})\big)$
  is an entrywise enclosure of $X$, equal to $(\tilde C,\tilde r)$ where
  $\tilde C$ is Hermitian and $\tilde r$ symmetric, so (i)--(ii) apply to
  it.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\end{technicalclaim}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Uses}\mref{Def.}{def:exact-reference}, \mref{Def.}{def:snap}
\metasep \metalabel{Used by}\extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/frank-wolfe/req:certified-evaluation}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/req:reference-companion}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep implemented (effective: accepted)
\metasep \metalabel{Code}\coderef{https://github.com/fraunhofersg/certiqs-key/blob/v0.1.0/src/certiqs_key/foundations/recentring.py}{certiqs_key.foundations.recentring:recentred_enclosure}}

\begin{proof}
(i) The real and imaginary parts of an entry of $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ are rationals
and $r_{il}$ is rational, so the inequality defining $Z$ is a comparison of
rationals, and $r'_{il}$ is a sum of rationals. For $(i,l)\in Z$,
\begin{equation*}
  |X_{il}-C'_{il}|=|X_{il}|\le|X_{il}-C_{il}|+|C_{il}|
  \le r_{il}+|\operatorname{Re}C_{il}|+|\operatorname{Im}C_{il}|=r'_{il},
\end{equation*}
by the triangle inequality, \eqref{eq:entrywise-enclosure} and
$|a+ib|\le|a|+|b|$; off $Z$ nothing changed. $C$ is Hermitian, so
$C_{li}=\overline{C_{il}}$, which has the same modulus and the same moduli of
real and imaginary part; with $r_{li}=r_{il}$ this gives
$(l,i)\in Z\iff(i,l)\in Z$ and $r'_{li}=r'_{il}$. On $Z$ both $C'_{il}$ and
$C'_{li}$ are $0=\overline{0}$, and off $Z$ they are $C_{il}$ and
$\overline{C_{il}}$, so $C'$ is Hermitian; a diagonal entry of $C$ is real
and stays real or becomes $0$.

(ii) For $(i,l)\in Z$, $|\operatorname{Re}C_{il}|+|\operatorname{Im}C_{il}|
\le\sqrt2\,|C_{il}|\le\sqrt2\,r_{il}$ by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality in
$\mathbb{R}^{2}$ and the definition of $Z$; off $Z$, $r'=r$. Where
$C_{il}=0$ the added term is $0$. An entry is structurally zero for an
enclosure exactly when its centre and its radius are both $0$
(Definition~\ref{def:snap}); such an entry lies in $Z$, keeps centre $0$ and
radius $0$, and an entry with centre or radius not zero keeps a radius not
zero or a centre not zero, since $r'_{il}\ge r_{il}$ and $C'_{il}\neq0$ only
off $Z$, where $C'_{il}=C_{il}$. Every entry of $Z$ has centre $0$ by
construction.

(iii) Definition~\ref{def:exact-reference} asks of a reference that its
blocks be Hermitian, positive semidefinite and complete at $c$, properties of
$G$ alone, and that each block be read with an entrywise enclosure with a
Hermitian centre in $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ and symmetric non-negative rational radii,
which (i) gives. The family $G$ is unchanged. Every radius of $(C,r)$ is $0$
exactly when every radius of $(C',r')$ is: if every $r_{il}=0$, an entry lies
in $Z$ only where $C_{il}=0$, so $r'=r$ by (ii); and $r'\ge r$ always.

(iv) The entries of $\tfrac12(\tilde C+\tilde C^{\dagger})$ are
$\tfrac12(\tilde C_{il}+\overline{\tilde C_{li}})\in\mathbb{Q}(i)$, the
matrix is Hermitian, and $\tfrac12(\tilde r_{il}+\tilde r_{li})$ is a
non-negative rational, symmetric in $(i,l)$. Since $X_{il}=\overline{X_{li}}$,
\begin{equation*}
  \Big|X_{il}-\tfrac12\big(\tilde C_{il}+\overline{\tilde C_{li}}\big)\Big|
  \le\tfrac12|X_{il}-\tilde C_{il}|+\tfrac12\big|\overline{X_{li}-\tilde C_{li}}\big|
  \le\tfrac12(\tilde r_{il}+\tilde r_{li}).
\end{equation*}
Where $\tilde C$ is Hermitian and $\tilde r$ symmetric, both averages return
them unchanged.
\end{proof}

% claim foundations/def:evaluated-off-snap
\claimsummary{foundations/def:evaluated-off-snap}{A declarer hands a reference beside a snap when it passes on the reference's centres and radii with it, unaltered. A block is evaluated off its snap when nothing its key length is computed from reads the snapped block, save the points and the values fixed before the first round.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/def:evaluated-off-snap}{Definition}{def:evaluated-off-snap}{A reference handed beside a snap; a block evaluated off its snap}
\claimleadin{%
A snap serves a run in two ways. A search reads the snapped family to find
points, and the numbers from which the run computes its key length read it
again at those points. The second reading is the one a premise about the snap
is needed for. A run that holds a \termref{term-reference}{reference} of the family can do the
second reading on a family that carries the reference in place of the snap,
and then the snap only steers the search: the points it chose are points like
any other, and a lower bound that holds at any admissible point holds at
them. The definition names the two things a record states when a run does
this: what the declarer passes on beside the snap, and on which blocks the
snapped data are read by nothing the key length rests on. Which values a
run of the engine fixes before its first round is listed in
\xref{meat-core/ass:fixed}; the definition names the values by that property
and does not depend on the list.
}
\begin{definition}[A reference handed beside a snap; a block evaluated off its snap]\label{def:evaluated-off-snap}
Let $F$ be a \termref{term-snap}{snap} (Definition~\ref{def:snap}) of data $D$ against a
\termref{term-sector-map}{sector map} with blocks $s\in\mathsf{S}$
(Definition~\ref{def:sector-map}), over an alphabet $J$, where $D$ is an
operator family read as a measurement, the data an instance states of it or a
reference of it, or a producer's exact construction of what it emits
(Definition~\ref{def:declared-data}).
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item Where $D$ is an operator family read as a measurement and the declarer
  holds a reference $G$ of it (Definition~\ref{def:exact-reference}), the
  declarer \emph{hands the reference beside the snap} on a block $s$ when it
  passes to every consumer of $F$, together with $F$ and altered by no step,
  the centre $C^{(s)}_j$, with entries in $\mathbb{Q}(i)$, and the radii
  $r^{(s)}_j$, rationals, of an entrywise enclosure of $G^{(s)}_j$ for every
  $j\in J$, with the identity of the reference and the claims that establish
  it. The reference so passed is the
  \termdef{term-handed-reference}{handed reference},
  and $s$ is a \emph{handed block}.
\item A block $s$ of $F$ is
  \termdef{term-evaluated-off-its-snap}{evaluated off its snap}
  in a run when the record of the run shows that no number from which the run
  computes its key length reads $F^{(s)}_j$ for any $j\in J$, save in two
  places: the points at which those numbers are evaluated, which any
  computation may have chosen, a computation on $F$ among them; and every
  value the run fixes before its first round other than the output length,
  the acceptance set and the transcript length $\lEC$ among them, whatever
  they were computed from.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Uses}\mref{Def.}{def:declared-data}, \mref{Def.}{def:sector-map}, \mref{Def.}{def:exact-reference}, \mref{Def.}{def:snap}
\metasep \metalabel{Used by}\mref{Ass.}{ass:snapped-measurement}, \mref{Req.}{req:who-snaps}, \mref{Req.}{req:snap-reference}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/frank-wolfe/req:bracket-on-reference}, \extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/rem:declared-measurement}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/detector-imperfections/rem:noise-floor-receiver}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/detector-imperfections/req:dark-composed-reference}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/cor:reference-companion}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/req:reference-companion}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep implemented (effective: accepted)
\metasep \metalabel{Code}\coderef{https://github.com/fraunhofersg/certiqs-key/blob/v0.1.0/src/certiqs_key/runs/direct_route.py}{certiqs_key.runs.direct_route:direct_route}}

\section{Domination and its limits}\label{group-foundations/def:domination}
\sectionintro{A family G dominates a family F at a block weight q when G \ensuremath{-} (1\ensuremath{-}q)F is positive semidefinite for every outcome; G is then a mixture of F and a complete \termref{term-residual-family}{residual family}, which is what lets a noise channel reduce G to F plus flags of weight q. A dominated family adds no support, though it may lose some, and domination composes and survives trusted classical post-processing (\hyperlink{claim-foundations/lem:domination}{Lemma~\ref*{lem:domination}}); for a family that absorbs its residue in one element only that element constrains the weight (\hyperlink{claim-foundations/lem:absorbing-domination}{Lemma~\ref*{lem:absorbing-domination}}). A reference can dominate a lattice family at a weight below one only along rationally spanned directions (\hyperlink{claim-foundations/lem:rational-obstruction}{Lemma~\ref*{lem:rational-obstruction}}), and an exact decision on a rational enclosure gives a sufficient condition for the positivity of matrices with irrational entries (\hyperlink{claim-foundations/lem:enclosure-psd}{Lemma~\ref*{lem:enclosure-psd}}). No requirement relates a snap to its model by domination; the section is kept for a declared device weight. The closing remark explains what a weight does not control, why an idealised model with an element whose support has no rational direction needs a noise floor before it dominates a lattice family at a small weight, and that reductions other than domination are not bound by that obstruction.}

% claim foundations/def:domination
\claimsummary{foundations/def:domination}{A family G dominates a family F at block weights q when G \ensuremath{-} (1\ensuremath{-}q)F is positive semidefinite for every outcome on every block, one weight per block. The residual family is what G holds beyond the weighted F, rescaled by the weight.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/def:domination}{Definition}{def:domination}{Domination of one operator family by another at block weights}
\claimleadin{%
Two \termref{term-exactly-admissible}{exactly admissible} measurements that are entrywise close can have key-rate
bounds far apart, by an amount the distance between them does not control
(\xref{meat-core/prop:optol-nobound}). A small change can alter which
outcomes a measurement treats as impossible on some direction, and a bound on
its size says nothing about that. Domination is a relation between two families
under which the dominated family gains no support; it bounds the dominated
family from above and not from below. It is the hypothesis under which a measurement $G$ is
a noise channel followed by $F$ together with classical flags of weight at
most $q_s$ on block $s$ \cite[Thm.~3, Eq.~(20)]{nahar2025imperfect}.
}
\begin{definition}[Domination of one operator family by another at block weights]\label{def:domination}
Let $\mathfrak{m}$ be a \termref{term-sector-map}{sector map} with blocks $s\in\mathsf{S}$ of
dimensions $d_s$ (Definition~\ref{def:sector-map}), let $J$ be a finite non-empty
alphabet, and let $G=\{G_j\}_{j\in J}$ and $F=\{F_j\}_{j\in J}$ be families of
\termref{term-block-list}{block lists} against $\mathfrak{m}$ whose blocks are
Hermitian and positive semidefinite; their entries are arbitrary complex
numbers. A family is \emph{complete at} a real number $c$ on block $s$ when
$\sum_{j\in J}G^{(s)}_j=c\,\idon{d_s}$. For weights $q=(q_s)_{s\in\mathsf{S}}$
with $q_s\in[0,1)$, the family $G$
\term[said of an operator family G and an operator family F over the same
alphabet and sector map, at block weights q in [0, 1): G − (1−q)F is positive
semidefinite for every outcome on every block, with the weight of that
block]{dominates} $F$ at $q$ when
\begin{equation}\label{eq:domination}
  G^{(s)}_j-(1-q_s)\,F^{(s)}_j\;\succeq\;0
  \qquad\text{for every }j\in J\text{ and }s\in\mathsf{S}.
\end{equation}
The weight $q_s$ belongs to the block $s$ and is the same for every outcome.
On a block $s$, the
\termdef{term-residual-family}{residual family} of the domination is
$R^{(s)}_j\coloneqq q_s^{-1}\big(G^{(s)}_j-(1-q_s)F^{(s)}_j\big)$ for
$j\in J$ where $q_s>0$, and $R^{(s)}_j\coloneqq G^{(s)}_j$ where $q_s=0$.
For a Hermitian matrix $X$ we write $\mathrm{supp}\,X$ for its range, the
orthogonal complement of its kernel.
\end{definition}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Uses}\mref{Def.}{def:sector-map}
\metasep \metalabel{Used by}\mref{Lem.}{lem:domination}, \mref{Lem.}{lem:absorbing-domination}, \mref{Lem.}{lem:rational-obstruction}, \mref{Rem.}{rem:noise-floor}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/domination/cor:dom-chain}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/domination/def:domination-link}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/domination/rem:rotated-projective}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/domination/thm:noise-channel}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep accepted}

% claim foundations/lem:domination
\claimsummary{foundations/lem:domination}{Domination is upward closed in the weight, holds below one exactly when each support of F lies in that of G, is equality at weight zero, composes multiplicatively and survives classical post-processing. G is then a mixture of F and a complete residual family.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/lem:domination}{Lemma}{lem:domination}{Elementary properties of domination}
\begin{lemma}[Elementary properties of domination]\label{lem:domination}
Let $\mathfrak{m}$, $J$ and the families $G=\{G_j\}_{j\in J}$,
$F=\{F_j\}_{j\in J}$ and $E=\{E_j\}_{j\in J}$ of block lists against
$\mathfrak{m}$ with Hermitian positive semidefinite blocks be as in
Definition~\ref{def:domination}, and let $s\in\mathsf{S}$ be a block.
Say that $G$ dominates $F$ at $q_s$ on block $s$ when
\eqref{eq:domination} holds at that block.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item \emph{(Upward closure.)} If $G$ dominates $F$ at $q_s$ on block $s$ and
  $q_s\le q'_s<1$, then $G$ dominates $F$ at $q'_s$ on block $s$.
\item \emph{(Support.)} If $G$ dominates $F$ at some $q_s\in[0,1)$ on block
  $s$, then $\mathrm{supp}\,F^{(s)}_j\subseteq\mathrm{supp}\,G^{(s)}_j$ for
  every $j\in J$. Conversely, if
  $\mathrm{supp}\,F^{(s)}_j\subseteq\mathrm{supp}\,G^{(s)}_j$ for every
  $j\in J$, then $G$ dominates $F$ on block $s$ at some weight in $[0,1)$.
\item \emph{(Weight zero.)} If $G$ and $F$ are both complete at the same
  $c$ on block $s$, then $G$ dominates $F$ at $0$ on block $s$ if and only
  if $F^{(s)}_j=G^{(s)}_j$ for every $j\in J$.
\item \emph{(Composition.)} If $G$ dominates $F$ at $q_s$ and $F$ dominates
  $E$ at $q'_s$ on block $s$, then $G$ dominates $E$ on block $s$ at
  $1-(1-q_s)(1-q'_s)$, which lies in $[0,1)$ and is at most $q_s+q'_s$.
\item \emph{(Classical post-processing.)} Let $W$ be a finite non-empty
  alphabet and let $P_{w|j}\ge0$ be real numbers for $w\in W$ and $j\in J$.
  Put $G'_w\coloneqq\sum_{j\in J}P_{w|j}G_j$ and
  $F'_w\coloneqq\sum_{j\in J}P_{w|j}F_j$, block by block. If $G$ dominates
  $F$ at $q_s$ on block $s$, then $G'$ dominates $F'$ at the same $q_s$ on
  block $s$. If moreover $\sum_{w\in W}P_{w|j}=1$ for every $j$ and $G$ and
  $F$ are complete at $c$ on block $s$, then so are $G'$ and $F'$. In
  particular, multiplying each $G_j$ and $F_j$ by the same number $p_j\ge0$
  preserves domination at the same weight.
\item \emph{(Residual family.)} If $G$ and $F$ are both complete at $c$ on
  block $s$ and $G$ dominates $F$ at $q_s$ there, then the residual family
  $R^{(s)}$ of Definition~\ref{def:domination} has positive semidefinite
  elements, is complete at $c$, and satisfies
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:residual-mixture}
    G^{(s)}_j=(1-q_s)\,F^{(s)}_j+q_s\,R^{(s)}_j
    \qquad\text{for every }j\in J.
  \end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Uses}\mref{Def.}{def:sector-map}, \mref{Def.}{def:domination}
\metasep \metalabel{Used by}\mref{Lem.}{lem:absorbing-domination}, \mref{Lem.}{lem:rational-obstruction}, \mref{Rem.}{rem:noise-floor}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/domination/rem:rotated-projective}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/domination/thm:noise-channel}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep accepted}

\begin{proof}
Throughout, fix the block $s$ and drop the superscript $(s)$.

(i) $G_j-(1-q'_s)F_j=\big(G_j-(1-q_s)F_j\big)+(q'_s-q_s)F_j$ is a sum of two
positive semidefinite matrices, the second because $q'_s-q_s\ge0$ and
$F_j\succeq0$.

(ii) Let $x\in\ker G_j$. Then
$0\le\langle x,(G_j-(1-q_s)F_j)x\rangle=-(1-q_s)\langle x,F_jx\rangle\le0$,
since $1-q_s>0$ and $F_j\succeq0$; so $\langle x,F_jx\rangle=0$. For a
positive semidefinite $F_j$ this gives $\|F_j^{1/2}x\|^2=0$, hence
$F_jx=F_j^{1/2}F_j^{1/2}x=0$. So $\ker G_j\subseteq\ker F_j$, and taking
orthogonal complements, $\mathrm{supp}\,F_j\subseteq\mathrm{supp}\,G_j$, both
matrices being Hermitian.
Conversely, suppose $\mathrm{supp}\,F_j\subseteq\mathrm{supp}\,G_j$ for every
$j$. For each $j$ with $F_j\neq0$, $G_j\neq0$ too; let $\Pi_j$ be the
orthogonal projector onto $\mathrm{supp}\,G_j$ and $\lambda_j>0$ the least
non-zero eigenvalue of $G_j$, so that $G_j\succeq\lambda_j\Pi_j$ by the
spectral decomposition. Since $F_j\preceq\opn{F_j}\,\idon{}$ and $F_j$ vanishes
on $(\mathrm{supp}\,G_j)^{\perp}\subseteq\ker F_j$, we have
$F_j=\Pi_jF_j\Pi_j\preceq\opn{F_j}\,\Pi_j\preceq t_jG_j$ with
$t_j\coloneqq\opn{F_j}/\lambda_j>0$. Put
$q_s\coloneqq\max\big(\{0\}\cup\{1-t_j^{-1}:F_j\neq0\}\big)$, which lies in
$[0,1)$. For $F_j=0$, $G_j-(1-q_s)F_j=G_j\succeq0$; for $F_j\neq0$,
$(1-q_s)t_j\le1$, so $(1-q_s)F_j\preceq(1-q_s)t_jG_j\preceq G_j$.

(iii) If $F_j=G_j$ for every $j$, \eqref{eq:domination} holds at $q_s=0$ with
equality. Conversely, if $G_j-F_j\succeq0$ for every $j$, then
$\sum_j(G_j-F_j)=c\,\idon{}-c\,\idon{}=0$ is a sum of positive semidefinite
matrices with trace $0$; each summand has non-negative trace, so each has
trace $0$, and a positive semidefinite matrix of trace $0$ is $0$. So
$F_j=G_j$ for every $j$.

(iv) Multiply $F_j-(1-q'_s)E_j\succeq0$ by $1-q_s\ge0$ and add
$G_j-(1-q_s)F_j\succeq0$: this gives $G_j-(1-q_s)(1-q'_s)E_j\succeq0$, which
is \eqref{eq:domination} for $G$ and $E$ at $1-(1-q_s)(1-q'_s)$. That weight
equals $q_s+q'_s-q_sq'_s$, which is at most $q_s+q'_s$ and at least $0$;
and $(1-q_s)(1-q'_s)>0$, so it is below $1$.

(v) Every $G'_w$ and $F'_w$ is Hermitian and positive semidefinite, being a
non-negative combination of such matrices, and
$G'_w-(1-q_s)F'_w=\sum_jP_{w|j}\big(G_j-(1-q_s)F_j\big)\succeq0$ for the same
reason. If every $\sum_wP_{w|j}=1$, then
$\sum_wG'_w=\sum_j\big(\sum_wP_{w|j}\big)G_j=\sum_jG_j=c\,\idon{}$, and the
same for $F'$. The case $p_j$ is $W=J$ with $P_{w|j}=p_j$ for $w=j$ and $0$
otherwise.

(vi) If $q_s>0$, then
$R_j=q_s^{-1}(G_j-(1-q_s)F_j)\succeq0$ by \eqref{eq:domination},
$\sum_jR_j=q_s^{-1}\big(c\,\idon{}-(1-q_s)c\,\idon{}\big)=c\,\idon{}$, and
$(1-q_s)F_j+q_sR_j=G_j$ by the definition of $R_j$. If $q_s=0$, then
$R_j=G_j\succeq0$ is complete at $c$, and $F_j=G_j$ by (iii), so
$(1-0)F_j+0\cdot R_j=G_j$.
\end{proof}

% claim foundations/lem:absorbing-domination
\claimsummary{foundations/lem:absorbing-domination}{When every element but one is rounded down below the reference element and the remaining one takes the rest, only that designated element constrains the weight. A weight below one exists exactly when the absorbed residue lies in its support, and it is at most residue norm over least eigenvalue.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/lem:absorbing-domination}{Lemma}{lem:absorbing-domination}{Domination of a family that absorbs its residue in one element}
\claimleadin{%
A family that keeps every element but one below its reference element and
lets one designated element take the rest is the simplest family a model can
dominate at a small weight. The lemma shows that the weight of the domination
is then decided by the designated element alone, and how large it is.
}
\begin{lemma}[Domination of a family that absorbs its residue in one element]\label{lem:absorbing-domination}
Let $s$ be a block of dimension $d_s$, $J$ a finite non-empty alphabet,
$c>0$, and $j^{\star}\in J$. Let $\{G_j\}_{j\in J}$ be Hermitian positive
semidefinite $d_s\times d_s$ matrices with $\sum_{j\in J}G_j=c\,\idon{d_s}$,
and let $\{F_j\}_{j\in J}$ be Hermitian matrices with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:absorbing}
  0\preceq F_j\preceq G_j\quad(j\neq j^{\star}),
  \qquad
  F_{j^{\star}}=c\,\idon{d_s}-\sum_{j\neq j^{\star}}F_j .
\end{equation}
Put $\Delta\coloneqq\sum_{j\neq j^{\star}}(G_j-F_j)$, the \emph{absorbed
residue}.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item $\Delta\succeq0$, $F_{j^{\star}}=G_{j^{\star}}+\Delta\succeq G_{j^{\star}}$,
  every $F_j$ is positive semidefinite, and $\sum_jF_j=c\,\idon{d_s}$.
\item For $q\in[0,1)$, $\{G_j\}$ dominates $\{F_j\}$ at $q$ on this block
  (Definition~\ref{def:domination}) if and only if
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:absorbing-condition}
    q\,G_{j^{\star}}-(1-q)\,\Delta\;\succeq\;0 .
  \end{equation}
  For every $j\neq j^{\star}$ and every $q\in[0,1)$,
  $G_j-(1-q)F_j\succeq0$ holds.
\item Some $q\in[0,1)$ satisfies \eqref{eq:absorbing-condition} if and only if
  $\mathrm{supp}\,\Delta\subseteq\mathrm{supp}\,G_{j^{\star}}$; this holds in
  particular when $G_{j^{\star}}$ is positive definite.
\item Suppose $\mathrm{supp}\,\Delta\subseteq\mathrm{supp}\,G_{j^{\star}}$,
  let $\lambda>0$ be the least non-zero eigenvalue of $G_{j^{\star}}$ (its
  least eigenvalue when it is positive definite) and let
  $\delta\ge\opn{\Delta}$. If $G_{j^{\star}}\neq0$, then
  \eqref{eq:absorbing-condition} holds for every $q$ with
  $\delta/(\lambda+\delta)\le q<1$. If $\Delta=0$, it holds at $q=0$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Uses}\mref{Def.}{def:domination}, \mref{Lem.}{lem:domination}
\metasep \metalabel{Used by}\mref{Rem.}{rem:noise-floor}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/domination/rem:rotated-projective}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep accepted}

\begin{proof}
(i) Each $G_j-F_j$ with $j\neq j^{\star}$ is positive semidefinite by
\eqref{eq:absorbing}, so $\Delta\succeq0$. By completeness of $\{G_j\}$,
$G_{j^{\star}}=c\,\idon{d_s}-\sum_{j\neq j^{\star}}G_j$, and subtracting this
from the definition of $F_{j^{\star}}$ gives
$F_{j^{\star}}-G_{j^{\star}}=\sum_{j\neq j^{\star}}(G_j-F_j)=\Delta$. So
$F_{j^{\star}}=G_{j^{\star}}+\Delta\succeq G_{j^{\star}}\succeq0$; the other
$F_j$ are positive semidefinite by \eqref{eq:absorbing}, and
$\sum_jF_j=c\,\idon{d_s}$ by the definition of $F_{j^{\star}}$.

(ii) For $j\neq j^{\star}$,
$G_j-(1-q)F_j=(G_j-F_j)+qF_j$ is a sum of two positive semidefinite
matrices, by \eqref{eq:absorbing} and $q\ge0$. For $j^{\star}$, by (i),
$G_{j^{\star}}-(1-q)F_{j^{\star}}=G_{j^{\star}}-(1-q)(G_{j^{\star}}+\Delta)
=qG_{j^{\star}}-(1-q)\Delta$. So \eqref{eq:domination} holds at every outcome
if and only if it holds at $j^{\star}$, which is
\eqref{eq:absorbing-condition}.

(iii) If \eqref{eq:absorbing-condition} holds for some $q<1$, then, by (ii),
$\{G_j\}$ dominates $\{F_j\}$ at $q$, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:domination}\,(ii) gives
$\mathrm{supp}\,F_{j^{\star}}\subseteq\mathrm{supp}\,G_{j^{\star}}$. Since
$0\preceq\Delta\preceq\Delta+G_{j^{\star}}=F_{j^{\star}}$, every
$x\in\ker F_{j^{\star}}$ satisfies $0\le\langle x,\Delta x\rangle\le
\langle x,F_{j^{\star}}x\rangle=0$, so $\Delta x=0$ as in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:domination}\,(ii); hence
$\mathrm{supp}\,\Delta\subseteq\mathrm{supp}\,F_{j^{\star}}\subseteq
\mathrm{supp}\,G_{j^{\star}}$. The converse is (iv) when $G_{j^{\star}}\neq0$
and $q=0$ when $\Delta=0$; if $G_{j^{\star}}=0$, the inclusion forces
$\Delta=0$. A positive definite $G_{j^{\star}}$ has support the whole space.

(iv) If $\Delta=0$, \eqref{eq:absorbing-condition} at $q=0$ reads $0\succeq0$.
Now let $G_{j^{\star}}\neq0$, and let $\Pi$ be the orthogonal projector onto
$\mathrm{supp}\,G_{j^{\star}}$. By the spectral decomposition
$G_{j^{\star}}\succeq\lambda\Pi$. Since $\mathrm{supp}\,\Delta\subseteq
\mathrm{supp}\,G_{j^{\star}}$ and $\Delta$ is Hermitian,
$\Delta=\Pi\Delta\Pi\preceq\opn{\Delta}\,\Pi\preceq\delta\,\Pi$. For
$q\ge\delta/(\lambda+\delta)$ we have $q\lambda\ge(1-q)\delta$, so
\begin{equation*}
  qG_{j^{\star}}-(1-q)\Delta\;\succeq\;q\lambda\,\Pi-(1-q)\delta\,\Pi
  \;=\;\big(q\lambda-(1-q)\delta\big)\Pi\;\succeq\;0 .
\end{equation*}
Since $\lambda>0$, $\delta/(\lambda+\delta)<1$, so such $q$ exist in
$[0,1)$.
\end{proof}

% claim foundations/lem:rational-obstruction
\claimsummary{foundations/lem:rational-obstruction}{A family with Gaussian-rational entries that G dominates at a weight below one has every support inside the largest rational subspace of the matching support of G. With completeness the weight is at least the largest value of G on the complement of that subspace, over the constant.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/lem:rational-obstruction}{Lemma}{lem:rational-obstruction}{Rationality obstruction to the domination of a lattice family}
\claimleadin{%
A lattice family has entries in the Gaussian rationals
$\mathbb{Q}(i)=\{x+iy:x,y\in\mathbb{Q}\}$. The lemma shows that such a family
can be dominated by a reference element, at a weight below one, only along
directions that rational vectors span, whatever its \termref{term-lattice-exponent}{lattice exponent}.
Domination itself does not depend on the basis, since a unitary applied to
both families preserves it; what depends on the basis is the lattice family,
whose entries are Gaussian rationals in the basis in which it is declared.
The lemma bounds the domination of such a family and nothing else. A
reduction that first applies a channel to the reference, such as a unitary,
changes the family that is compared with a lattice family: the lemma then
applies to the image of the reference, whose supports may have rational
directions that those of the reference lacked
(Remark~\ref{rem:noise-floor}).
}
\begin{lemma}[Rationality obstruction to the domination of a lattice family]\label{lem:rational-obstruction}
Let $d\ge1$, and read every vector of $\mathbb{C}^{d}$ and every
$d\times d$ matrix in the standard basis. Call a subspace $U$ of
$\mathbb{C}^{d}$ \emph{$\mathbb{Q}(i)$-rational} when it is spanned over
$\mathbb{C}$ by vectors of $\mathbb{Q}(i)^{d}$ (the subspace $\{0\}$ is
spanned by the empty set), and for a subspace $V$ of $\mathbb{C}^{d}$ put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-part}
  \mathcal{R}(V)\;\coloneqq\;\mathrm{span}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(V\cap\mathbb{Q}(i)^{d}\big),
\end{equation}
the \emph{largest $\mathbb{Q}(i)$-rational subspace of $V$}.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item $\mathcal{R}(V)$ is a $\mathbb{Q}(i)$-rational subspace contained in
  $V$, and it contains every $\mathbb{Q}(i)$-rational subspace contained in
  $V$.
\item For every $d\times d'$ matrix $A$ with entries in $\mathbb{Q}(i)$, the
  range of $A$ is $\mathbb{Q}(i)$-rational. In particular the support of a
  Hermitian $d\times d$ matrix with entries in $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ is.
\item Let $\{G_j\}_{j\in J}$ and $\{F_j\}_{j\in J}$ be Hermitian positive
  semidefinite $d\times d$ matrices over a finite non-empty alphabet $J$,
  every $F_j$ with entries in $\mathbb{Q}(i)$, such that
  $G_j-(1-q)F_j\succeq0$ for every $j$, for some $q\in[0,1)$. Then
  $\mathrm{supp}\,F_j\subseteq\mathcal{R}_j\coloneqq
  \mathcal{R}(\mathrm{supp}\,G_j)$ for every $j$.
\item If, in (iii), moreover $\sum_jG_j=\sum_jF_j=c\,\idon{d}$ with $c>0$,
  then for every $j\in J$
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:rational-bound}
    q\;\ge\;\frac{\lmax\big(P_jG_jP_j\big)}{c},
  \end{equation}
  where $P_j$ is the orthogonal projector onto $\mathcal{R}_j^{\perp}$.
\item In particular, if $\mathrm{supp}\,G_j$ contains no non-zero vector of
  $\mathbb{Q}(i)^{d}$, then $q\ge\lmax(G_j)/c$, which equals $\tr G_j/c$
  when $G_j$ has rank one.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Uses}\mref{Def.}{def:domination}, \mref{Lem.}{lem:domination}
\metasep \metalabel{Used by}\mref{Rem.}{rem:noise-floor}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/detector-imperfections/rem:noise-floor-receiver}, \extref{../reductions/contract.pdf}{reductions/domination/rem:rotated-projective}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep accepted}

\begin{proof}
(i) $V\cap\mathbb{Q}(i)^{d}\subseteq V$ and $V$ is a subspace, so the span
lies in $V$; it is spanned by vectors of $\mathbb{Q}(i)^{d}$ by its
definition. If $U\subseteq V$ is spanned by vectors
$u_1,\dots,u_m\in\mathbb{Q}(i)^{d}$, each $u_l$ lies in
$U\cap\mathbb{Q}(i)^{d}\subseteq V\cap\mathbb{Q}(i)^{d}$, so
$U\subseteq\mathcal{R}(V)$.

(ii) The range of $A$ is $\{Ax:x\in\mathbb{C}^{d'}\}$, and
$Ax=\sum_lx_lAe_l$, so it is the span of the columns $Ae_1,\dots,Ae_{d'}$ of
$A$, each a vector of $\mathbb{Q}(i)^{d}$. For a Hermitian matrix the support
is the range (Definition~\ref{def:domination}).

(iii) By Lemma~\ref{lem:domination}\,(ii), applied to the one-block families
$\{G_j\}$ and $\{F_j\}$ at weight $q<1$,
$\mathrm{supp}\,F_j\subseteq\mathrm{supp}\,G_j$. By (ii) $\mathrm{supp}\,F_j$
is $\mathbb{Q}(i)$-rational, so by (i) it lies in
$\mathcal{R}(\mathrm{supp}\,G_j)$.

(iv) Fix $j$. Summing $G_l-(1-q)F_l\succeq0$ over $l\neq j$ and using both
completeness identities,
\begin{equation*}
  0\;\preceq\;\big(c\,\idon{d}-G_j\big)-(1-q)\big(c\,\idon{d}-F_j\big)
  \;=\;qc\,\idon{d}-G_j+(1-q)F_j .
\end{equation*}
Let $\varphi\in\mathcal{R}_j^{\perp}$ be a unit vector. By (iii),
$\mathrm{supp}\,F_j\subseteq\mathcal{R}_j$, so $\varphi$ is orthogonal to the
range of the Hermitian matrix $F_j$ and therefore lies in its kernel; hence
$\langle\varphi,F_j\varphi\rangle=0$, and the display gives
$\langle\varphi,G_j\varphi\rangle\le qc$. Now let $x\in\mathbb{C}^{d}$ be any
unit vector. If $P_jx=0$, then $\langle x,P_jG_jP_jx\rangle=0\le qc$.
Otherwise $\varphi\coloneqq P_jx/\|P_jx\|$ is a unit vector of
$\mathcal{R}_j^{\perp}$ and $\|P_jx\|\le1$, so
$\langle x,P_jG_jP_jx\rangle=\|P_jx\|^{2}\langle\varphi,G_j\varphi\rangle\le qc$.
Since $P_jG_jP_j$ is Hermitian, its largest eigenvalue is the maximum of
$\langle x,P_jG_jP_jx\rangle$ over unit vectors $x$, which is therefore at most
$qc$.

(v) Under the hypothesis, $\mathrm{supp}\,G_j\cap\mathbb{Q}(i)^{d}=\{0\}$, so
$\mathcal{R}_j=\{0\}$ and $P_j=\idon{d}$, and \eqref{eq:rational-bound} reads
$q\ge\lmax(G_j)/c$. A positive semidefinite matrix of rank one has one
non-zero eigenvalue, which is its trace.
\end{proof}

% claim foundations/lem:enclosure-psd
\claimsummary{foundations/lem:enclosure-psd}{A Hermitian matrix is at least \ensuremath{\mu} times the identity when a Gaussian-rational centre within entrywise radii r is at least \ensuremath{\rho} + \ensuremath{\mu} times it, \ensuremath{\rho} the largest row sum of r. Every hypothesis is a comparison of rationals, so matrices with irrational entries are decided in exact arithmetic.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/lem:enclosure-psd}{Lemma}{lem:enclosure-psd}{Positive semidefiniteness from an entrywise enclosure}
\claimleadin{%
A matrix with irrational entries, such as one with entries
$S_{il}/\sqrt{n_in_l}$, is not a matrix of rationals, and an exact decision of
its positive semidefiniteness cannot read its entries directly. The lemma replaces the decision by one on a rational centre, at the
price of a margin. It is a sufficient condition only: a matrix whose least
eigenvalue is smaller than the uncertainty of its enclosure is in general not
certified, and a finer enclosure is the remedy.
}
\begin{lemma}[Positive semidefiniteness from an entrywise enclosure]\label{lem:enclosure-psd}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item Let $X$ be a Hermitian complex $d\times d$ matrix, $X_c$ a Hermitian
  $d\times d$ matrix with entries in $\mathbb{Q}(i)$, and $r_{il}\ge0$
  rationals with $|X_{il}-(X_c)_{il}|\le r_{il}$ for all $i,l$. Let $\rho$ be
  a rational with
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:enclosure-radius}
    \rho\;\ge\;\max_{i}\sum_{l}r_{il}
    \qquad\text{or}\qquad
    \rho\ge0\ \text{ and }\ \rho^{2}\;\ge\;\sum_{i,l}r_{il}^{2},
  \end{equation}
  and $\mu\ge0$ a rational. If $X_c-(\rho+\mu)\,\idon{d}\succeq0$, then
  $X\succeq\mu\,\idon{d}$; in particular $X\succeq0$, and $X$ is positive
  definite when $\mu>0$. If $X_c-\rho\,\idon{d}$ is positive definite, then
  $X$ is positive definite. Every hypothesis on $X_c$, $r$, $\rho$ and $\mu$
  is a property of finitely many rationals and Gaussian rationals.
\item Let $n_1,\dots,n_d$ be positive rationals and
  $D\coloneqq\mathrm{diag}(\sqrt{n_1},\dots,\sqrt{n_d})$, and let $a_i,e_i$
  be rationals with $0\le e_i\le a_i$ and
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:sqrt-enclosure}
    (a_i-e_i)^{2}\,n_i\;\le\;1\;\le\;(a_i+e_i)^{2}\,n_i .
  \end{equation}
  Then $|a_i-n_i^{-1/2}|\le e_i$. Let $S$ and $Y$ be Hermitian $d\times d$
  matrices with entries in $\mathbb{Q}(i)$, put $X\coloneqq D^{-1}SD^{-1}-Y$,
  $A\coloneqq\mathrm{diag}(a_1,\dots,a_d)$, $X_c\coloneqq ASA-Y$ and
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:scaled-radii}
    r_{il}\;\coloneqq\;\sigma_{il}\,\big(a_ie_l+e_ia_l+e_ie_l\big),
    \qquad
    \sigma_{il}\coloneqq|\mathrm{Re}\,S_{il}|+|\mathrm{Im}\,S_{il}| .
  \end{equation}
  Then $X$, $X_c$ and $r$ satisfy the hypotheses of (i) on $X$, $X_c$ and
  $r$, and the radii do not depend on $Y$.
\item Let $X$, $X_c$ and $r$ be as in (i), let $F$ be a Hermitian positive
  semidefinite $d\times d$ matrix with entries in $\mathbb{Q}(i)$, and let
  $q\in[0,1]$ be rational. Then $X-(1-q)F$, $X_c-(1-q)F$ and $r$ satisfy the
  hypotheses of (i) on $X$, $X_c$ and $r$. If, for some $\rho$ and $\mu$ as
  in (i), $X_c-(1-q)F-(\rho+\mu)\idon{d}\succeq0$, then
  $X_c-(1-q')F-(\rho+\mu)\idon{d}\succeq0$ for every rational
  $q'\in[q,1]$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Used by}\extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/thm:exact-and-evaluated}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep implemented
\metasep \metalabel{Code}\coderef{https://github.com/fraunhofersg/certiqs-key/blob/v0.1.0/src/certiqs_key/foundations/reference.py}{certiqs_key.foundations.reference:enclosure_psd}}

\begin{proof}
(i) Put $Z\coloneqq X-X_c$, a Hermitian matrix, so $|Z_{il}|=|Z_{li}|$. Then
$|Z_{il}|\le r'_{il}\coloneqq\min(r_{il},r_{li})$, and $r'$ is symmetric with
$\sum_lr'_{il}\le\sum_lr_{il}$ for every $i$. Let $x\in\mathbb{C}^{d}$ be a
unit vector. If $\rho\ge\max_i\sum_lr_{il}$, then, using
$|x_i||x_l|\le\tfrac12(|x_i|^{2}+|x_l|^{2})$ and the symmetry of $r'$,
\begin{equation*}
  |\langle x,Zx\rangle|
  \le\sum_{i,l}|x_i|\,r'_{il}\,|x_l|
  \le\tfrac12\sum_{i,l}r'_{il}\big(|x_i|^{2}+|x_l|^{2}\big)
  =\sum_i|x_i|^{2}\sum_lr'_{il}
  \le\max_i\sum_lr_{il}\le\rho .
\end{equation*}
If instead $\rho\ge0$ and $\rho^{2}\ge\sum_{i,l}r_{il}^{2}$, the
Cauchy--Schwarz inequality on the $d^{2}$ numbers $r_{il}$ and
$|x_i||x_l|$ gives
\begin{equation*}
  |\langle x,Zx\rangle|\le\sum_{i,l}r_{il}\,|x_i||x_l|
  \le\Big(\sum_{i,l}r_{il}^{2}\Big)^{1/2}\Big(\sum_{i,l}|x_i|^{2}|x_l|^{2}\Big)^{1/2}
  =\Big(\sum_{i,l}r_{il}^{2}\Big)^{1/2}\le\rho ,
\end{equation*}
since $\sum_{i,l}|x_i|^{2}|x_l|^{2}=\big(\sum_i|x_i|^{2}\big)^{2}=1$. In both
cases $\langle x,Xx\rangle=\langle x,X_cx\rangle+\langle x,Zx\rangle
\ge(\rho+\mu)-\rho=\mu$, because $X_c-(\rho+\mu)\idon{d}\succeq0$. As $X$ is
Hermitian and $x$ was an arbitrary unit vector, $X\succeq\mu\,\idon{d}$. If
instead $X_c-\rho\,\idon{d}$ is positive definite, the same bounds on
$|\langle x,Zx\rangle|$ give
$\langle x,Xx\rangle\ge\langle x,X_cx\rangle-\rho
=\langle x,(X_c-\rho\,\idon{d})x\rangle>0$ for every unit vector $x$, so $X$
is positive definite. The
hypotheses are a finite set of comparisons of rationals and the positive
semidefiniteness of the matrix $X_c-(\rho+\mu)\idon{d}$ with entries in
$\mathbb{Q}(i)$.

(ii) The map $t\mapsto t^{2}n_i$ is strictly increasing on $[0,\infty)$, and
$a_i-e_i\ge0$, $n_i^{-1/2}>0$, $(n_i^{-1/2})^{2}n_i=1$; so
\eqref{eq:sqrt-enclosure} gives $a_i-e_i\le n_i^{-1/2}\le a_i+e_i$. Write
$n_i^{-1/2}=a_i+\varepsilon_i$ with $|\varepsilon_i|\le e_i$. The entry
$(i,l)$ of $D^{-1}SD^{-1}$ is
$S_{il}(a_i+\varepsilon_i)(a_l+\varepsilon_l)$, and that of $ASA$ is
$S_{il}a_ia_l$, so
\begin{equation*}
  |X_{il}-(X_c)_{il}|
  =|S_{il}|\,\big|a_i\varepsilon_l+\varepsilon_ia_l+\varepsilon_i\varepsilon_l\big|
  \le\sigma_{il}\,\big(a_ie_l+e_ia_l+e_ie_l\big)=r_{il},
\end{equation*}
using $a_i,a_l\ge0$ and $|z|\le|\mathrm{Re}\,z|+|\mathrm{Im}\,z|$. The matrix
$X$ is Hermitian, $D^{-1}$ being real diagonal and $S$, $Y$ Hermitian; $X_c$
is Hermitian with entries in $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ for the same reasons; the $r_{il}$
are non-negative rationals, and $Y$ does not enter them.

(iii) $X-(1-q)F$ is Hermitian, and $X_c-(1-q)F$ is Hermitian with entries in
$\mathbb{Q}(i)$, $q$ being rational and $F$ having entries in
$\mathbb{Q}(i)$. Since
$\big(X-(1-q)F\big)_{il}-\big(X_c-(1-q)F\big)_{il}=X_{il}-(X_c)_{il}$, the
radii $r$ still bound the differences entry by entry. Finally,
$X_c-(1-q')F-(\rho+\mu)\idon{d}
=\big(X_c-(1-q)F-(\rho+\mu)\idon{d}\big)+(q'-q)F$ is a sum of two positive
semidefinite matrices, since $q'-q\ge0$ and $F\succeq0$.
\end{proof}

% claim foundations/rem:noise-floor
\claimsummary{foundations/rem:noise-floor}{A weight at which a model dominates a lattice family shows that the family adds no support, not how far it lowers an element. An element with no rational direction in its support forces a weight of at least its top eigenvalue over the constant; noise in the model removes that bound.}
\claimbookmark{foundations/rem:noise-floor}{Remark}{rem:noise-floor}{What domination controls, and why it needs a noise floor}
\claimleadin{%
No requirement of the engine relates a snapped family to its model by
domination: a run evaluates the numbers its key length rests on with the
model in place of the snap where it holds one, and rests on a named premise
elsewhere. The remark says what domination would control if a weight were
declared or established, and why an idealised model could not be related to
a lattice family that way at a small weight. Reductions other than domination
that could reduce an idealised model exactly, and a declared device weight,
are future scope (\href{../../../spec/future-scope.md}{\nolinkurl{spec/future-scope.md}}~\S13).
}
\begin{remark}[What domination controls, and why it needs a noise floor]\label{rem:noise-floor}
Let $G$ be a \termref{term-reference}{reference} (Definition~\ref{def:exact-reference}) and $F$
a family of the same shape whose entries are \termref{term-lattice-value}{lattice
values}, both complete at $c$, with $G$ dominating $F$ at a weight $q<1$
(Definition~\ref{def:domination}). The relation bounds every element of $F$
from above by its reference element, $(1-q)F_j\preceq G_j$. What that bound
controls, and what it does not, comes first. Three facts then decide when the
weight can be small, and together they explain when an idealised model whose
elements are rank-deficient dominates no lattice family at a small weight,
what a declaration should do instead, and why that obstruction belongs to
domination and not to every reduction.

\emph{What domination controls.} The relation of
Definition~\ref{def:domination} is the hypothesis under which the reference
is a noise channel followed by $F$, together with classical flags of
weight at most $q_s$ on block $s$ \cite[Thm.~3, Eq.~(20)]{nahar2025imperfect}.
Domination bounds each element of $F$ from above and not from below: $F$
may lower the probability of an outcome, and may remove support, making
impossible an outcome that the model makes possible, at a weight below the
lattice step. For one block of dimension one with $c=1$,
$G_1=2^{-k}/3$ and $G_2=1-2^{-k}/3$, the only lattice value at $k$ in
$[0,2^{-k}/3]$ is $0$, and the family $F_1=0$, $F_2=1$ that rounds $G_1$
down and lets $G_2$ take the rest is dominated at every $q\ge2^{-k}/3$,
since $G_1-(1-q)F_1=G_1\succeq0$ and $G_2-(1-q)F_2=q-2^{-k}/3$, although
outcome~$1$ has become impossible.

\emph{Support.} At a weight below one, an element of $F$ has no support
outside that of its reference element (Lemma~\ref{lem:domination}\,(ii)): for
$x$ in the kernel of $G_j$,
$0\le\langle x,(G_j-(1-q)F_j)x\rangle=-(1-q)\langle x,F_jx\rangle$, so
$F_jx=0$. An outcome that the model makes impossible on some direction stays
exactly impossible there, so an element of $F$ must fit inside the support of
its reference element, and that is what a lattice family can fail to do at a
small weight.

\emph{Rationality.} A lattice family has Gaussian-rational entries in the
basis in which it is declared, so the support of each of its elements is
spanned by Gaussian-rational vectors. A dominated element therefore lies in
the largest rational subspace $\mathcal{R}_j$ of the support of $G_j$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:rational-obstruction}\,(iii)), and completeness turns this
into the lower bound $q\ge\lmax(P_jG_jP_j)/c$, with $P_j$ the projector onto
the orthogonal complement of $\mathcal{R}_j$
(Lemma~\ref{lem:rational-obstruction}\,(iv)). The bound depends on the basis
in which the lattice family is declared and not on the lattice exponent: a
finer lattice still has Gaussian-rational entries, so no refinement of the
lattice lowers it.

\emph{An example at two photons.} Take two orthogonal polarisation modes $H$
and $V$ and the two-photon block in the orthonormal occupation basis
$\ket{2,0},\ket{1,1},\ket{0,2}$. With the diagonal mode created by
$a_D^{\dagger}=(a_H^{\dagger}+a_V^{\dagger})/\sqrt2$, the state with both
photons in that mode is
\begin{equation*}
  \ket{DD}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big(a_D^{\dagger}\big)^{2}\ket{0,0}
  =\tfrac12\ket{2,0}+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\ket{1,1}+\tfrac12\ket{0,2},
\end{equation*}
since $(a_H^{\dagger})^{2}\ket{0,0}=\sqrt2\ket{2,0}$ and
$a_H^{\dagger}a_V^{\dagger}\ket{0,0}=\ket{1,1}$. For an ideal, lossless
analyser in the diagonal basis without dark counts, the element of the
outcome in which only the detector of $D$ clicks is $\dyad{DD}$ on this block.
Every non-zero vector on that ray has second coordinate $\sqrt2$ times its
first, so none has Gaussian-rational coordinates, $\mathcal{R}_j=\{0\}$, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:rational-obstruction}\,(v) gives $q\ge\tr\dyad{DD}/c=1/c$:
with $c=1$ no lattice family declared in this basis is dominated by the
model at a weight below one, whatever the lattice exponent. Such irrational
directions are common in photon-number blocks of two or more photons,
because the occupation basis carries factors $1/\sqrt{n}$; the diagonal basis
already produces one.

\emph{A noise floor removes the obstruction.} A physical detector has loss and
dark counts. In a model that includes both in every port, no outcome is
impossible on a photon-number block, and, under conditions that the module
modelling the detector states, every element is positive definite on every
block. Supports are then no obstruction: let every element of $F$ but one
lie between zero and its reference element and let the remaining one, chosen
positive definite in the reference, take what completeness leaves; the
reference then dominates $F$ at a weight of at most $\delta/(\lambda+\delta)$,
where $\delta$ is the norm of the residue the remaining element absorbs and
$\lambda$ the least eigenvalue of the reference element at that outcome, not
of the element of $F$, which the residue raises above it
(Lemma~\ref{lem:absorbing-domination}\,(iv)).
When the other elements stay within a few lattice steps of their reference
elements, $\delta$ is of the order of the lattice step times the number of
outcomes and the dimension, and the weight is of the order of that over
$\lambda$. Loss alone or dark counts alone need not suffice: what matters is
that no element is rank-deficient on a block, and a model in which some
outcome is still impossible on some block keeps the obstruction for that
element.

\emph{Declaring the floor.} A weight relates $F$ to the model $G$ and says
nothing about whether $G$ describes the device; that is the premise of the
declaration's own model. A larger floor makes $\lambda$ larger and the
weight smaller, which is a temptation and not a licence: a floor above the
noise the device has makes the model wrong, an error no weight can show. The
floor to declare is the smallest loss and dark-count rates one is sure the
device has.

\emph{Rank deficiency alone is no obstruction.} A block whose elements are
rank-deficient but have supports spanned by Gaussian-rational vectors may be
dominated by its model at a weight of the order of the lattice step. For one
block of dimension two with $c=1$ and
$G_1=\mathrm{diag}(3/5,0)$, $G_2=\mathrm{diag}(2/5,0)$,
$G_3=\mathrm{diag}(0,1)$, put $a\coloneqq\lfloor2^{k}\cdot3/5\rfloor\,2^{-k}$
and $F_1=\mathrm{diag}(a,0)$, $F_2=\mathrm{diag}(1-a,0)$, $F_3=G_3$. Then
$G_1-(1-q)F_1$ and $G_3-(1-q)F_3$ are positive semidefinite for every
$q\in[0,1)$, and $G_2-(1-q)F_2\succeq0$ exactly when
$q\ge(3/5-a)/(1-a)$, which is below $\tfrac52\,2^{-k}$ because
$0\le3/5-a<2^{-k}$ and $1-a>2/5$, although no element is positive definite.
Where the support of some element contains no non-zero Gaussian-rational
vector, no lattice family is dominated below the bound of
Lemma~\ref{lem:rational-obstruction}\,(v) at any lattice exponent; there it
is the noise floor, not a finer lattice, that makes a small weight possible.

\emph{What the obstruction does not say.} Domination compares the reference
with $F$ element by element on the same block, and the channel it yields acts
on each block as the identity followed by a branching into $F$ and flags. A
unitary applied to both families preserves domination; what fixes the basis
is the lattice family, Gaussian-rational in the basis in which it is
declared. Lemma~\ref{lem:rational-obstruction} bounds the domination of such
a family and nothing else. A reduction that first applies another channel can
map some idealised models exactly onto a family with Gaussian-rational
entries, with no direction to snap at all. An ideal analyser whose analysed
polarisation $\cos\alpha\ket{H}+\sin\alpha\ket{V}$ has an irrational
$\tan\alpha$, so that its one-photon element has no Gaussian-rational
direction in its support, is the image, under one unitary applied to the
input of every outcome, of the same analyser at an angle at which its
elements are lattice values, such as $\alpha=0$. On the block of $m$ photons
in two modes, the isometry from that block into the $m$-fold tensor power of
$\mathbb{C}^{2}$, which maps $\ket{2,0}$, $\ket{1,1}$ and $\ket{0,2}$ to
$\ket{HH}$, $(\ket{HV}+\ket{VH})/\sqrt2$ and $\ket{VV}$, carries $\ket{DD}$ of
the example above to $\tfrac12(\ket{HH}+\ket{HV}+\ket{VH}+\ket{VV})$, which
has rational coordinates, at dimension $2^{m}$ instead of $m+1$. Such
reductions are not claims of this module; an idealised model that dominates
no lattice family at a small weight may still be reducible exactly by them.
\end{remark}
\claimmeta{\metalabel{Uses}\mref{Def.}{def:exact-reference}, \mref{Def.}{def:domination}, \mref{Lem.}{lem:domination}, \mref{Lem.}{lem:absorbing-domination}, \mref{Lem.}{lem:rational-obstruction}
\metasep \metalabel{Used by}\extref{../meat-core/contract.pdf}{meat-core/rem:declared-measurement}, \extref{../receiver/contract.pdf}{receiver/detector-imperfections/rem:noise-floor-receiver}
\metasep newly derived
\metasep accepted}

\section{The exact island, enclosures and the tiers}\label{group-foundations/def:exact-island}
\sectionintro{The \termref{term-exact-island}{exact island} is where the engine computes on exact rationals, namely every decision that data satisfy the conditions their declaration states, a snap's decisions on its output and the decisions on a reference among them, a producer's construction of its emission, the exact establishment of the acceptance-side iterate and of the acceptance-side minimum over the acceptance set as its consumer reads it, and the certification of a lower bound on the feasible-side minimum. A least eigenvalue is bounded from below exactly from any approximate eigenbasis, by a Gershgorin bound corrected for the basis' defect from orthogonality (\hyperlink{claim-foundations/lem:least-eigenvalue-bound}{Lemma~\ref*{lem:least-eigenvalue-bound}}).
